knowledge.evidence: Conservation agriculture (CA) incorporates crop management practices that can enhance productivity while conserving natural resources and improving soil physical properties. To assess this, an experiment was conducted during 2021–22 and 2022–23 at ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi to evaluate soil physical properties and their impact on crop productivity in a long-term CA-based maize (Zea mays L.)–wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) system, initiated in 2010. The CA-based treatments were zero tillage with and without residue (ZT and ZT + R); permanent broad bed with and without residue (PBB and PBB + R); permanent narrow bed with and without residue (PNB and PNB + R) and conventional tillage (CT). The treatments were laid out under a randomised complete block design (RCBD) with three replications. Over the top 15 cm of soil, there was a 7.8% reduction in bulk density (BD) across the residue plots over non-residue plots. Although the highest porosity was observed in PNB + R (36.7%), all CA-based treatments were statistically comparable. The core auger method, as described by Blake and Hartge (1986), was used to estimate soil bulk density (BD). knowledge.evidence: Effect of conventional tillage (CT) and conservation agriculture (CA)-based practices on soil physical properties Bulk density and porosity: Tillage, residue and crop establishment practices had a notable impact on soil bulk density (BD) across all soil depths (Fig. 1A). With increasing soil depth, BD increased significantly. BD in the 0–15cm soil layer ranged from 1.36 (PBB + R) to 1.59 Mg/m3 (CT) with an average of 1.45 Mg/m3. PBB + R registered a 14.2% lower value than CT, whereas other CA-based treatments demonstrated significantly lower BD (5.5–12.5%) than CT. Most significantly, ZT + R and PNB + R showed 11.1% and 12.5%, respectively lower BD than CT but there was no substantial (p<0.05) difference between the two. Similar outcomes have been reported by Raj et al. (2023) for bed- planting systems under long-term conservation practices. Over the top 15 cm of soil, there was a 7.8% decrease in BD across the residue plots over non-residue plots including CT. Similarly, in the 15–30 cm soil layer, the maximum BD was observed in CT (1.75 Mg/m3) and the lowest in PBB + R (1.57 Mg/m3). CA has shown to enhance soil physical health (Jat et al. 2009, Indoria et al. 2017, Bhattacharya et al. 2023), soil organic carbon, hydraulic properties of soil (Maity et al. 2011), root water uptake, ecosystem services (Mandal et al. 2025), soil moisture conservation, and reduce water footprints (Bhattacharya et al. 2020). The total area under conservation agriculture in different parts of South Asia is around 2.5 mha (Jat et al. 2020) and the area area is mostly confined to rice–wheat based cropping system. The detailed knowledge of the long-term impacts of various tillage and planting methods, as well as of straw retention on soil physical properties and crop yield in MWS within the IGP, remains insufficient. This study was carried out to evaluate the effect of various tillage, residue management, and crop establishment options on crop productivity and soil physical properties of an MWS in the IGP region. knowledge.evidence: The current study was carried out during 2021–22 and 2022–23 at ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi (28°35´N, 77°12´E; at an elevation of 229 m amsl) on a long-term maize–wheat field experiment initiated in 2010 based on conservation agriculture. The experimental location is characterised by a semi-arid subtropical climate, featuring dry, hot summers and cold, wet winters. The highest temperatures are recorded in May while the lowest occurs in January. The experimental site's soil is categorised as Typic Haplustept. At the start of the experiment, the top 0–15 cm layer had a pH of 7.8 and a sandy clay loam texture. Available P was at 24.3 kg/ha, available K was at 251.5 kg/ha, oxidisable SOC was at 5.3 g/kg, EC was 0.63 dS/m and oxidisable N content was at 183.3 kg/ha. knowledge.evidence: Salinity and sodicity severely limit the productivity of the rice-wheat system (RWS) in the Indo-Gangetic Plains. Conservation Agriculture (CA) practices offer potential to restore soil health and sustain yields under such constraints. A five-year (2015–2020) on-farm study was conducted at four sites in Haryana, namely Geong, Sambhli, Bhaupur and Kaith, under varying saline and sodic environments. Four management scenarios (SCs) combining tillage, residue, and irrigation were evaluated namely: (Sc-1) puddled transplanted rice – conventional tillage wheat (conventional farmer’s practice; PTR–CTW), (Sc-2) PTR + wheat residue incorporation – CTW + rice residue mulch, (Sc-3) reduce tillage direct seeded rice (RTDSR) + wheat residue incorporation – zero- tillage wheat (ZTW) + rice residue mulch under surface irrigation, and (Sc-4) RTDSR + wheat residue incorporation – ZTW + rice residue mulch under sprinkler irrigation. The salt-tolerant varieties Basmati CSR 30 (rice) and KRL 210 (wheat) were used as test crop. Pooled analysis revealed that sprinkler-based RTDSR– ZTW with residue retention achieved the highest system productivity (9.6 Mg ha-¹ yr-¹), outperforming the conventional practice by 15–18%. Rice and wheat yields increased by 11 and 17.8%, respectively. The findings

The application of 100% NPK + 10 tonnes FYM/ha + lime incorporation at the rate 100% lime requirement (LR) increased the stover and grain yield by 161 and 179% over 100% NPK, respectively. The quality parameters like crude protein content (10.10%), P content (0.42%), Ca content (0.27%) and Mg content (0.14%) were also recorded higher with application of 100% NPK along with FYM (10 t/ha) and lime (100% LR). The results suggested the importance of sustainable soil fertility management, particularly the beneficial effects of integrating chemical fertilizer with lime and FYM in improving maize yield, nutrient uptake, and grain quality, compared to the sole use of chemical fertilizers in an acidic soil.

In acid soils aluminium toxicity first affects root growth and then nutrient uptake and consequently above ground biomass accumulation (Sierra et al. 2003). Monitoring soil pH is crucial for achieving optimum crop productivity. The use of lime is a potential option for the sustainable management of soils to increase the productivity of maize (Bharti et al. 2021, Islam et al. 2021). Hence, achieving higher maize yield along with maintaining soil health and sustainability requires a proper soil management approach involving the judicious use of fertilizers, manures and amendments. Current research lacks comprehensive strategies for optimizing the use of organic amendments like FYM and lime with chemical fertilizers to enhance nutrient uptake, grain quality and productivity in acidic soils. The study aims to address these gaps by investigating the combined effects of these amendments, offering insights into sustainable nutrient management, and region-specific strategies for enhancing maize productivity in acidic soils.

source.title: Effect of farmyard manure, fertilizers and lime on quality parameters, nutrient uptake and productivity of maize (Zea mays) in acidic condition of north-western Himalayas

knowledge.evidence: Experimental site: A field experiment was conducted during rainy (kharif) seasons of (June to October) 2020 and 2021 at Research Farm of Chaudhary Sarwan Kumar Krishi Vishvavidyalaya (32ᵒ7ʹ N and 76ᵒ31ʹ E, with an altitude 1290 m amsl), Palampur, Himachal Pradesh. The soil of the study area was silt loam in texture (Typic Hapludalf) with an acidic pH (5.49), medium in organic carbon (0.83%), and available N (291 kg/ha), P (11.2 kg/ ha) and K (228 kg/ha). The average rainfall received during the crop growth period was 80.5 mm in 2020 and 110.5 mm in 2021. The minimum and maximum temperatures were 14.6 and 30.5°C in kharif 2020 and 14.9 and 31.1°C in kharif 2021, respectively. Experimental details: Maize variety, K-25 Gold was sown in the second week of June in a plot size of 12 m2 with a spacing of 60 cm × 15 cm for both the seasons. K-25 Gold is a recommended variety in the north-western Himalayan region. The experiment was conducted in a randomized complete block design (RCBD), comprised of 11 treatments, viz. T1, Control; T2, 100% NPK; T3, 100% NPK + 5 t FYM/ha; T4, 100% NPK + 10 t FYM/ha; T5, 100% NPK + lime (full dose through broadcasting); T6, 100% NPK + lime (1/10th dose through furrow application);

knowledge.evidence: Yield: The findings from the two-year data (2020 and 2021) depicted that the average yield of maize grain ranged between 6.2 to 50.1 q/ha, whereas the yield of straw varied from 11.3–77.1 q/ha (Table 1). The application of two different levels of FYM, 5 t FYM/ha (T3) and 10 t FYM/ha (T4) along with 100% NPK recorded 35.2 and 86.6% higher grain yield over 100% NPK alone, respectively. The stover yield followed similar trend as that of the grain yield under various treatments. The highest grain and stover yield were recorded with the combined use of 100% NPK along with the FYM @10 t/ha and lime incorporation @100% LR (T8), followed by the treatment involving same combination but with lime incorporation @1/10th LR in furrow (T10). The treatments T8 recorded 87.65 and 85.31% higher grain and stover yield over control (T1), respectively. The combined use of farmyard manure (FYM), lime, and fertilizers led to the maximum production of both maize grain and stover. The addition of FYM releases organic acids that can bind with aluminium and iron, consequently reducing phosphorus (P) retention and enhancing P availability, thereby promoting greater maize growth and productivity. knowledge.evidence: Water and nutrient holding capacities are primarily controlled by the secondary soil parameters of water retention characteristics and cation exchange capacities (CEC). Complete suite of these secondary soil parameters is rarely included in legacy soil databases generated in soil survey and mapping efforts. Therefore, pedotransfer functions (PTF) are generally used to derive these parameters. We used PTFs and laboratory-measured water contents at field capacity (θFC) and wilting points (θPWP) and CEC values to augment the existing Indian soil legacy database that contained CEC data for 1681 locations and θFC and θPWP data for about a 3rd of these lo­ cations across the country. A quantile regression forest (QRF) algorithm was used to map these three soil pa­ rameters at six GlobalSoilMap-specified soil depths. Estimated coefficient of determination (R2) values in the 10- fold cross-validated datasets ranged from 0.60 to 0.65 for CEC while a substantially lower accuracies were found for the water holding capacities (R2 for θFC: 0.27–0.34 and R2 for θPWP: 0.33–0.37). Terrain attribute showed stronger influence on the distribution of these secondary soil parameters than the climatic parameters. Specifically, valley depth showed strongest negative correlation coefficients (r: −0.68 to −0.73) with layer-wise CEC values; January temperature showed strongest influence on water holding capacities (r: 0.08 to 0.62 with θFC and 0.14 to 0.62 for θPWP). Thus, CEC in Indian soils is primarily driven by the pedo­ genesis of clays in which monsoon rain favors clay translocation to deeper soil layers followed by subsequent deposition in subsurface horizons during the post-monsoon dry weathers. Similarly, strong linkages between January temperature and water holding capacities reaffirm the conclusion that temperature of driest quarters is a key driver of water relationships in soil.

knowledge.evidence: Soil as a multifunctional medium for plant growth is increasingly recognized as a key component of achieving sustainable development goals (Blum, 1993; European Commission, 2006; Banwart, 2011; Baveye et al., 2016; Evans et al., 2021). Soils directly contribute to 9 out of 17 sustainable development goals (Keesstra et al., 2016). Specifically, biomass production, storage and filtration of water, storage and recy­ cling of nutrients, carbon storage and habitat for biological activity are considered major ecological functions of soils (Wiesmeier et al., 2019). Each of these functions are closely linked to the capability of a soil to sustain and increase food production – a compelling requirement in many countries including in India where farm income is mandated to double by 2022 (Chand, 2017). Improved management practices and agricultural intensification are needed to realize such goals; but, inten­ sification has been shown to cause the deterioration in soil quality (Squire et al., 2015). However, conventional measurement methods for secondary soil properties are expensive and time-consuming (Romano and Palladino, 2002; Malone et al., 2020) and, therefore, most legacy soil databases often do not contain these important soil properties for all soil profiles or their individual horizons. Consequently, pedotransfer functions (PTF) are frequently used for deriving secondary soil proper­ ties from basic soil properties (Bouma, 1989; van Looy et al., 2017). Because legacy databases provide soil data for a specific location (point data), soil mapping is done to obtain soil properties at unmeasured locations. Over the last few decades, digital soil mapping (DSM) approaches have been developed to provide soil information and inferences in a continuous manner (McBratney et al., 2003; Malone et al., 2009; Minasny et al., 2013). A seminal work to estimate soil hydraulic properties from soil surface area in the PTF approach dates back to 1966 (Abrol and Khosla, 1966). However, development of parametric PTFs for hydraulic properties using basic soil properties (Santra and Das 2008; Adhikary et al., 2008; Santra et al., 2018) or through reflectance spectroscopy (Santra et al., 2009) and the use of machine learning approaches for Indian soils (Jena et al., 2021) are fairly recent although most of these studies have been conducted over small geographical areas. No national-scale mapping efforts exist for understanding the nature and distribution of water holding capac­ ities of this vast subcontinent. Preliminary modelling studies using multiple linear regression (MLR) and several machine learning approaches showed that secondary soil properties may be readily estimated using the random forest (RF; Breiman, 2001) and extreme gradient boosting (XGB) algorithms (Chen and Guestrin, 2016). The RF model follows a bagging algorithm in which each node is split using the best among a subset of predictors randomly chosen at that node following a bootstrap approach (Breiman, 2001). The XGB algorithm involves an ensembling technique where we build many independent models and combine them using model averaging technique (Chen and Guestrin, 2016). We used the randomforest and xgboost to implement the above modelling approaches in the R software (R Core Team, 2019) and RStudio 1.0.153 (RStudio Team, 2015). For the predictor variables, we tested basic soil properties and different environmental covariates (Table S3) in multiple combinations. Results showed that the addition of environmental covariates to the basic soil properties did not improve the performance of the developed PTFs.

With the available legacy CEC data for 1681 profile locations, scenario 1 provided DSM estimates of CEC at each profile locations; thus, the RMSE values (4.42 to 4.75 cmolc kg−1) esti­ mated using observed and DSM-estimated CEC values for these 1681 locations represent the extent of error because of DSM model itself. Estimated RMSE values for scenario 2 (4.23–4.52 cmolc kg−1) suggest that the combination of PTF and DSM reduced the total error. The RMSE values of 4.48–4.66 cmolc kg−1 from the scenario 3 (the approach fol­ lowed for estimating missing θFC and θPWP values in the legacy dataset in our study) lie in between those for scenario 2 and scenario 1. These results suggest that the use of PTF may actually reduce the total error during DSM modelling. Nevertheless, we emphasize that the creation of legacy data with high soil profile density is a prime requirement for decreasing the 90 % prediction interval in for estimating soil properties using the DSM approach.

knowledge.evidence: influence of clay contents and soil pH on the nutrient retention capacity (CEC) are consistent with the well-known facts that soil structure majorly influences soil water relationships while charge characteristics (permanent and pH-dependent) influences cation exchange behavior in soil. Soils with high SOC and clay contents are known to have large and stable soil aggregates (Bronick and Lal, 2005; Purushothaman et al., 2022); soils with such stable aggregates are expected to have high available water contents. Thus, both θFC and θPWP are expected to be positively correlated to both clay and SOC contents because of their role in the formation and stabilization of soil aggregates. With moderate to strong weathering intensities, soil pH values < 7 were observed in 3681 out of 7317 soil layers (~50 %) used in this study suggesting the pres­ ence of iron and aluminum oxides and hydroxides, which contributes to soil aggregation (Bronick and Lal, 2005; Sarathjith et al., 2014; Vasava et al., 2019). Negative correlation coefficients between soil pH and water holding capacities may be a result of low pH-mediated influence of Fe- and Al- oxides and hydroxides on soil aggregation.

knowledge.evidence: Legacy soil data and measured soil properties from different sources were combined with terrain and bioclimatic variables and vegetation indices using machine learning and digital soil mapping approaches to develop digital soil maps for water and nutrient holding capacities for Indian soils for six GlobalSoilMap-specified depths at 500 m resolution. Original legacy soil data were available for 1681 locations for CEC across the country while about a third of these locations had θFC and θPWP data. Because RF models and bioclimatic factors have shown promise to fill such data gaps, we used a machine learning framework to create national-scale soil maps for these secondary soil properties. Similar to many DSM studies, estimated R2 values in the 10-fold cross- validated datasets ranged from 0.60 to 0.65 for CEC while a substan­ tially lower accuracies were found for the water holding capacities (R2 for θFC: 0.27–0.34 and R2 for θPWP: 0.33–0.37). Resulting soil function maps show distinct spatial patterns that are closely linked to the parent material and bioclimatic variables consistent with the scorpan frame­ work. knowledge.evidence: Mapping of soil micronutrient variability is critical for improving agronomic biofortification. This study used 1778 surface soil samples collected from four agro-climatic regions of the Indo-Gangetic Plain of India to produce digital soil maps of available Zn, Cu, Fe, and Mn using 52 environmental covariates at a resolution of 150 m. The micronutrient prediction accuracy was compared for 14 machine learning approaches and their ensemble model. The hybrid ensemble model outperformed all 14 base learners and was subsequently used for producing micronutrient maps. All four micronutrients exhibited sufficient spatial variability. Both available Zn and Fe maps exhibited lower prediction uncertainties. Moreover, the inter-relationship between micronutrient con­ centration in soil and rice grain was explored to understand the Zn and Fe biofortification potential. The linear regression models revealed moderate agreement between soil available and grain micronutrient concentrations, with R2 values of 0.52–0.63 for Zn and Fe, respectively. A common option for soil pH and SOC raster layer is GlobalSoilGrids at the 250 m × 250 m spatial resolution (Hengl et al., 2017). However, these layers were created from a global legacy soil database and may not be very accurate at a local scale, depending upon sampling density in the study area. Moreover, the layers may not highlight the current soil conditions as the legacy data­ sets have been collected at least a decade back. Therefore, in-situ measured soil pH and SOC content at sampled locations were interpo­ lated into uniform spatial grids of 150 m × 150 m using the Kriging method. A spherical model with non-zero nuggets was used for fitting the variogram (supplementary material, Figs. SM-1 and 2).

knowledge.evidence: Over the last decade, ensemble ML method has gained popularity in almost all fields, including quantifying the soil spatial relationships. In the ensemble learning method, several algorithms were combined in a single model to maximize the prediction accuracy, which showed a higher prediction power than the individual models (Rojas et al., 2008; Malone et al., 2014). Subsequently, individual predictions from each base learner and their weighted average represent the final ensemble model. In this study, all feature selection and modeling were performed using the “caret” and “caretEnsemble” packages in R 3.5.2 (R Devel­ opment Core Team, 2020). The box and density plots of the original dataset exhibited that the data had a wide range with some extreme outliers and were non-normally distributed for all the micronutrients. Consequently, the Tukey Krammer approach (Tukey, 1977) was implemented using the “transformTukey()” function from the R package rcompanion (Mangiafico, 2016), which iteratively uses the Shapiro-Wilk test for finding suitable λ value to convert the non-normally distributed data to normal. knowledge.evidence: Descriptive statistics for four analyzed soil micronutrients, using original vales, along with soil pH and SOC (%), are presented in Table 4. All micronutrients exhibited wide variability, indicating variation in parent material, geology, vegetation, local management practices, soil biota, and topography throughout the study area (Bhunia et al., 2018). In addition, the soil pH of the study area also varied widely (3.10–8.90) from strongly acidic to highly alkaline, suggesting the influence of soil reaction on spatial variability of micronutrients (Brady and Weil, 2002). Moreover, the SOC (%) of the sampled soils also showed wide variability (0.11–2.37%). Notably, the RLZ and VAZ exhibited mean SOC values of 0.61% and 0.63%, respectively, which resulted from continuous crop­ ping without applying adequate organic matter in these soils over the years (Patra et al., 2014). In contrast, the CSZ and GAZ exhibited moderate to high SOC, with a mean of 0.96% and 0.82%, respectively. As expected, the coefficient of variation (CV) of the SOC for the four agro-climatic zones varied widely from 28 to 65%. The mean availability of the analyzed micronutrients followed the order: Fe > Mn > Cu > Zn.

Under a tropical, intense leaching environment, topography-driven erosional processes accelerate soil nutrient transport through rain­ water and sediment across the slope (Hounkpatin et al., 2022). Many studies have concluded that terrain attributes are valuable predictors of soil nutrients (Zeraatpisheh et al., 2019, Tajik et al., 2020). Likewise, the relative influence of terrain-derived covariates was distinct for all micronutrients (Fig. 5). Channel networks base level, multi-resolution ridge-top flatness index, and channel networks distance were the most influential terrain parameters. Yet, the relative superiority of climatic variables over terrain parameters can stem from the fact that the elevation was somewhat uniform across these agro-climatic regions and therefore was not the most dominant controlling factor. Furthermore, the spatial variability of relatively immobile micronutrients is governed by their solubility in soil solution. Geochemical drivers like redox po­ tential, pH, soil minerals, organic matter, and nutrient interactions mainly determine micronutrient availability in soil solution (Dhaliwal et al., 2019). The intense and frequent rainfall pattern of CSZ can explain the elevated level of soil micronutrients. Indeed, precipitation influences several geochemical reactions under a specific pH range which changes metal solubility from soluble (e.g., Zn2+, Fe3+, and Mn2+) to insoluble phases (e.g., Zn- carbonate, Fe, and Mn hydroxides) (Sauv´e et al., 2000; Moreno- Jim´enez et al., 2019). Among remote sensing-based indices, EVI, related to vegetation greenness, exhibited a positive association with available Mn concentration. Vegetation indices had the potency to explore the soil variability due to the close association between soil properties and vegetation (Falahatkar et al., 2016). The positive effect of SOC on available Fe (Fig. 6) can be attributed to the chelating ability of SOM (Gungor and Let, 2010) and the production of organic acids, which offer favorable pH for micronutrient availability (Zhao et al., 2018).

The linear regression models revealed moderate agreement be­ tween soil available and grain micronutrient concentrations, with R2 values of 0.52 to 0.63 for Zn and Fe, respectively (Fig. 9). Similar agreement was observed for rice straw, with R2 values of 0.59 to 0.68 for Zn and Fe, respectively. The developed models were used for spatially predicting grain Zn and Fe content from their respective soil concen­ tration in parts of the VAZ (Fig. 10). Results revealed that most areas in the VAZ had low grain Zn level, that is less than the targeted Zn level in rice grains. However, in the case of grain Fe content, areas of the eastern part of the VAZ, covering South 24 Parganas, exhibited higher levels of grain Fe than other parts. The spatial variation map of grain Zn and Fe can help in identifying specific pockets where rice varieties with bio­ fortification potential can be planted. This will also enable identifying areas where specific mitigation strategies should be taken for enhancing the micronutrient content in rice grains. However, rice grain processing causes a considerable loss of Zn and Fe (>60%) and eventually results in minimal human consumption (Saha et al., 2015).

However, the detailed soil surveys are most often scarce on large territories, which generates clustered calibration sets that may not represent the whole unmapped area. It is therefore important to delineate extrapolation areas that have soil-landscape relationships sufficiently similar to those of the soil map perimeter. Soilscape distances were then used to select the appropriate DSM model for predicting soil property classes at each location (i.e. the model calibrated with the map of the closest micro-watershed). Soilscape distances served also to delineate extrapolation areas around existing soil maps in which soil property classes can be predicted with the highest accuracy and lowest predicted uncertainty. Using a leave-one-micro-watershed-out evaluation approach, We found that a single model calibrated onto the entire set of soil maps successfully predicted the texture and stoniness classes of soils over an extrapolation area covering 7% of the entire study area. Accuracies of 94% and 90% were obtained for texture, and stoniness, with respective predicted uncertainties of 6% and 7%. However, lower accuracy (57%) and higher uncertainty (31%) were obtained for predicted soil depth classes. Using multiple DSM models, each selected from soilscape dis­ tances, did not improve upon these results. This exploratory study paves the way for a possible hybrid approach to mapping soils across large territories.

The first two soil properties to be predicted were expressed in the soil map as ordinal variables (depth classes and stoniness) with known underlying contin­ uous variables (depth and stone content). The latter, soil texture, is not normally expressed by ordinal classes. However, in this particular case, the soil texture classes could be considered as ordinal because they were ordered according to the clay content (Table 1), which was the under­ lying continuous variable. As we did in a previous study using the same type of soil data as input (Lagacherie et al., 2025), we followed the recommendation of Hornung (2019). We converted the three soil properties into continuous variables by assigning the midpoint of the intervals defining their ordinal classes. For depth and stone content, we considered the explicitly defined in­ tervals of quantitative values (Table 1). knowledge.evidence: 4 (Fridland, 1974). Soilscapes have recently been considered as a suitable underlying concept for the delineation of soil districts in Europe (Wadoux et al., 2024). Following this earlier work, we have chosen to describe soilscapes quantitatively by calculating the distribution of soil classes within each micro-watershed, which is considered here as the elementary soil landscape unit. Based on this quantitative representation of a soilscape, the soilscape distance between two micro-watersheds was defined by i) calculating the Euclidean distances between the depth, texture and stoniness class distributions of two given watersheds and ii) combining the three Euclidean distances thus obtained into a single one by simply averaging them. 4095 soilscape distances between the 91 micro-watersheds with soil maps were calculated using a specific R script. These distances were further considered as the ground-truth soilscape distances.

Predictions were more accurate when a single model calibrated onto the entire set of soil maps was used, as opposed to multiple models, each calibrated onto a single soil map and selected by choosing the one with the minimum soilscape distance. The errors affecting the predicted soilscape distances previously observed had a significant impact on the performance of the multiple model approach, as the prediction accuracy decreased when using predicted rather than ground-truth soilscape distances. knowledge.evidence: The use of legacy soil maps as input for DSM models to map soil properties has rarely been considered in the literature. To the best of our knowledge, only Bui and Moran (2003) deviated from the common practice of using legacy site soil observations and measurements to produce broad scale DSM products (Arrouays et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2022). However, their approach in the Murray-Darling Basin in Australia involved filling the gaps between a small number of soil maps at various scales that already covered most of the study area. This differs greatly from our attempt to extrapolate from very detailed soil maps that together cover only a tiny part of the study area (0.33%). The performance of the single model's predictions, when using the entire set of soil maps, can be compared with other attempts to map soil property classes over areas of similar size. knowledge.evidence: The presented approach is one of the rare DSM approaches that explicitly considers one upper level of organisation of the soil cover. This level is referred to here as 'soilscape', although it has been widely re­ ported by soil scientists around the world under different terms (Astle et al., 1969; Fridland, 1974; Favrot, 1981; Smeck et al., 1983). This level has also been used as the basis for defining the mapping units of con­ ventional small-scale soil maps (Bornand et al., 1989; Costantini et al., 2012). Previously, Brungard et al. (2021) tested an ensemble of indi­ vidual DSM models, each calibrated within a well-defined eco-physio­ graphic region, as an alternative to the traditional single model calibrated across the entire mapped area. This assumes that each eco- physiographic region has specific soil-landscape relationships. Wadoux et al. (2024) used the concept of soilscapes to map soil districts in Europe, aggregating soilscapes quantitatively represented as distribu­ tions of continental-scale soil units or soil covariates. knowledge.evidence: In this study, we compared the performance of two adverse DSM approaches: using all the available soil maps to build a single model, or using each soil map separately to build multiple models and then selecting the correct model based on the soilscape distance between the micro-watershed with the soil map and the micro-watershed to be mapped. Overall prediction performance (Table 3) showed that the single model approach clearly outperformed the multiple model approach. However, when focusing on micro-watersheds closest to those with soil maps (Fig. 4), the two approaches performed similarly (Fig. 5). Never­ theless, inaccurate predictions of soilscape distances (Fig. 3) restored the superiority of the single model approach, even for the closest micro- watersheds (Fig. 6). In the future, it could be interesting to consider an intermediate approach between those tested in this paper. Following Brungard et al. (2021), this approach would consist of building an ensemble model based on a combination of weighted single models. These weights could then be determined using the soilscape distance probabilities predicted by the random forest.

knowledge.evidence: This study builds on past and ongoing soil inventory programmes that have, until now, relied solely on detailed, traditional soil surveys of micro-watersheds. We have paved the way for a new approach for mapping soils over large territories with high precision while main­ taining acceptable time and cost constraints. This is particularly true for soil properties that can be mapped in detail and are well-correlated with soil covariates, such as texture and stoniness class, as demonstrated in this study. This hybrid approach would combine conventional surveying over limited areas with a DSM approach for extrapolating the detailed soil maps to the rest of the territory. In this perspective, we demon­ strated in the Karnataka state that a small number of mapped micro- watersheds (91), representing a small cumulative area (464 km2), could be extrapolated to cover a much larger area (10,892 km2) using DSM. knowledge.evidence: Rice-wheat cropping system (RWCS) is the most important system occupying around 26 M ha spread over the Indo Gangetic Plains in South Asia and China. Many long-term trials were led to assess the agronomic produc­ tivity and economic profitability of various combinations of conservation agricultural (CA) practices (zero tillage, residue management and crop establishment) in RWCS of Eastern Indo-Gangetic Plains (EIGP) of India. The purpose of this study was to investigate the best management practices involving different tillage-based crop establishment and residue retention techniques and their contribution to agricultural system sustainability through improvement in soil health by developing soil quality index (SQI). We have used SQI as an instrument based on physical [macro aggregate stability (MAS), available water capacity (AWC) and soil penetration resistance (SPR)], chemical [soil organic carbon (OC), available N, available P and available K] and biological [microbial biomass carbon (MBC), fluorescein diacetate (FDA) and dehydrogenase activity (DHA)] properties of soil, because these are very useful indicators of soil’s functions for agronomic productivity and soil fertility. Integration of several soil properties to soil quality indices can provide a better picture of soil quality than indi­ vidual parameters. Further one should select soil indicators that interact synergistically which can help in measuring the soil quality and stability under different crop cultivation practices. Doran, 2002 defined soil quality as the capacity of a soil to function and promote plant and animal productivity, and maintain or enhance water and air quality. Mainte­ nance and promotion of soil quality is, therefore, a fundamental requirement to ensure ecosystem sustainability. knowledge.evidence: Physical, chemical and biological properties of mean soil layer (0-20 cm) were subjected to PCA. The result showed that 79.96% of the total variance was explained by two principal components (PCs) (Table 4) with eigenvalues greater than one. The PC-1 and PC-2 described 62.61 and 17.3% of the variability, respectively. Since the majority of the data information explained by PC-1 allows differentiation between different management practices applied to plots. In biplot, the location of soil properties and different treatments scattered in different regions of PCA axes is on the basis of the correlation coefficient between variables, treatments occupying opposite places in the diagram i.e. in the opposite direction of an axis show distinct variations (Fig. 1). The variables that are largely accountable for this variation can be observed by simulta­ neously projecting scores (treatments) and loading (variables) onto PC-1 axis (Fig. 1). Variables like FDA, DHA, MBC, SOC, AWC and MAS were positively correlated (close) to plots where zero/reduced tillage prac­ tices were adopted, whereas all these variables (soil properties) were negatively correlated to conventional tillage treatments (Fig. 1).

knowledge.evidence: Soil physical parameter like, aggregate stability is considered as the main soil physical indicator as it depicts the soil’s ability to resist me­ chanical disruption that may lead to soil erosion. It influences other soil properties like soil porosity, soil structure, water holding capacity, organic matter stability and elemental bio-cycling (Ghildyal and Tri­ pathi, 1987; Gelaw et al., 2015). The amount of carbon in soil strongly influences the aggregate stability. Doran (1987) observed less oxidative soil environment under zero tillage practice than conventional tillage, which favours the carbon stabilization in such soils. We observed that treatments having ZT and RT with residue retention on the surface enabled the safety of organic matter from microbial degradation due to lesser soil disruption, which in turn favoured the generation of physi­ cally stable macro-aggregates (Mondal et al., 2019). Similar observa­ tions have been reported by Sarker et al. (2018). Tillage caused the breakdown of macro-aggregate to finer aggregates and facilitated the degradation of exposed organic matter present in the soil, thus reduced soil aggregation, making the soil more sensitive to wind or water erosion

The higher yield recorded in T7 and T6 highlights the beneficial role of ZT/RT and surface residue retention practices. These results showed that under identical nutrient management conditions, tillage based crop establishment systems with different residue man­ agement determine the soil physical and biochemical indices. knowledge.evidence: Pedology, the study of pedogenesis, includes soil classification and mapping. Digital soil mapping (DSM) has evolved from traditional methods to creating comprehensive spatial soil information systems. This advancement is achieved by integrating field and laboratory data with environmental covariates and incorporating new geotechnologies such as geophysical techniques and remote sensing data, alongside machine learning ap­ proaches. This integration in DSM provides novel insights into soil survey and mapping, offering detailed in­ formation on soil variability both vertically and laterally. It also raises new research questions that traditional pedology may not have addressed. In this study, we proposed and compared three strategies for DSM in Brazil, creating predictive pedological mapping. These strategies integrate data from three geophysical sensors, remote sensing data, relief, and lithology as input in a machine learning approach testing five algorithms. knowledge.evidence: Information about the set of attributes that different types of soil possess is essential for various practical purposes related to sustainable land use and management. Such information is obtained through the classification and delimitation of the spatial distribution of soils, accomplished through survey work and pedological mapping (IUSS Working Group WRB, 2015). Inaccurate soil classification and mapping can lead to inappropriate soil use and management, resulting in harmful impacts on the environment and agriculture, forestry, and zootechnical production systems (Duniway et al., 2010). Pedological mapping involves identifying and classifying soil types and their spatial distribution within a given geographic area (Rodrigo- Comino et al., 2018). Soil is defined as product of the interaction among soil formation factors identified by Dokuchaev (1967) and later formalized by Jenny (1941) as climate, organisms, relief, parent mate­ rial, and time. Consequently, soil types vary spatially and temporally because their morphological attributes result from anisotropic geolog­ ical, morphogenetic, and pedogenetic processes (Breemen and Buur­ man, 2003). It relied on the interpretation of aerial photos, topographic maps, vegetation, and field observations, to create polyg­ onal class maps of soil, assuming discrete boundaries between them (Hudson, 1992; Minasny and McBratney, 2016). The second approach, digital soil mapping (DSM), has emerged in the early 2000's following great advances in geotechnologies and computational capability (McBratney et al., 2003a). DSM accepts variability within soil classes and produces contour maps that reflect gradual transition zones. As a quantitative approach, DSM extends the classical soil formation factor equation to include new factors, providing a range of values for soil physical-chemical, mineralogical, and biological attributes using advanced statistical theories (Lagacherie et al., 2006; McBratney et al., 2003b). knowledge.evidence: 2.2.1. Gamma-ray survey Soil gamma-ray spectrometric characterization was conducted using a proximal-surface gamma-ray spectrometer (GM), the RS 230 model by Radiation Solution Inc. (Ontario, Canada). This instrument measures eTh and eU in parts per million (ppm), while K40, due to its relative abundance in the soil, is reported in percentage. Standard units for radionuclide concentrations are mg kg−1 for eU and eTh, and percentage for K40. The GM spectrometer detects gamma-ray emissions to a depth of 30–60 cm, with detection depth varying due to factors like soil bulk density and moisture (Beamish, 2015; Taylor et al., 2002; Wilford, 1997). Initially, the GM was calibrated by placing it on the ground surface and leaving it active for five minutes, allowing the readings of eU, eTh, and K40 levels to stabilize (Solutions, 2009). Radionuclide measure­ ments were taken using the “assay mode” for maximum precision, with the GM positioned at the soil surface for two minutes at each of the 183 sampling points. Geographic coordinates for each point were recorded with a GPS integrated into the GM (GPS – Radiation Solution Inc., Ontario, Canada) with a precision of 1 m.

knowledge.evidence: 2.2.2. Magnetic susceptibility (κ) survey For soil κ analysis, measurements were taken at all 183 sampling points using a geophysical susceptibility meter (KT10 – Terraplus). This device measures κ to a depth of 2 cm below the surface with a precision of 10−6 SI units, expressed in m3 kg−1. To ensure accuracy, the sensor was calibrated by first determining the frequency of the outdoor oscil­ lator. Readings were then conducted in three sequential steps: (1) recording the frequency and amplitude of the oscillator in free air; (2) placing the coil directly on the soil surface to measure frequency and amplitude on the sample; and (3) repeating the initial free-air mea­ surement and displaying results. Details on these procedures can be found in (Sales, 2021). Measurements were taken in scanner mode, optimizing the geometric correlation for direct κ readings to achieve rapid and accurate results. Three readings were conducted in a trian­ gular pattern around each sampling point, and the mean κ value was used in all analyses to minimize noise.

Apparent electrical conductivity (ECa) survey We conducted the soil ECa measurements using the Geonics EM38 conductivity meter (Geonics Ltd., Mississauga, Ontario, Canada) (McNeill, 1986). The EM38 measures quad-phase conductivity (in m S m−1) without requiring direct soil contact (Geonics, 2002). Calibration followed the protocol described by Heil and Schmidhalter (2019), Sec­ tion 3.1.1, as ECa values depend on calibration settings, coil orientation, and coil separation (Heil and Schmidhalter, 2019). Further operational details on the EM38 can be found in Hendrickx et al. (2002). Following calibration, ECa readings were taken at each of the 183 sampling points using a vertical dipole orientation, which provides data from an effective depth of approximately 1.5 m. Field data were collected during the dry season on bare soil and at consistent intervals to minimize environ­ mental influences. To prevent interference, all metal objects were kept at a distance from the EM38 during readings. Fig. 2. knowledge.evidence: The SYSI is an approach that combines multi-temporal satellite im­ ages to create a single synthetic image representing soil characteristics over time. SYSI typically identifies bare soil through multi-temporal analysis, selecting images or pixels from periods when vegetation cover is minimal or absent. These bare soil observations are then inte­ grated over time to build the synthetic SYSI image, ensuring that the soil signal is strong and representative of the underlying properties. The system involves acquiring satellite images from different periods to capture seasonal and temporal variations, processing these images to correct distortions and align them, and integrating the processed data into a comprehensive synthetic representation. Machine learning algo­ rithms and statistical models are then applied to analyze the integrated data, allowing the identification and quantification of soil attributes such as texture, moisture, and mineral composition. This approach provides detailed and accurate information for digital soil mapping, precision agriculture, and sustainable land management (Demattˆe et al., 2018). knowledge.evidence: Although our study provides valuable insights into different digital soil mapping strategies by combining remote sensing, geophysical data, and soil formation factors (relief and lithology), it does have some limitations. First, the covariates used as input data in the predictive pedological mapping model (geophysical data, relief attributes, and SYSI) may not fully capture the spatial and temporal variability of soil formation factors, processes, and mapping units. This limitation arises from the resolution and availability of field-collected data. Second, while the Random Forest model proved effective, it assumes indepen­ dence between predictors and is susceptible to overfitting, particularly given the relatively small size of our training dataset. Third, the refer­ ence data used for model validation were derived from classical soil mapping methods, whose error rates were not quantified. Although the Agreement/Disagreement method offers appropriate statistical support for validation, this lack of error quantification may introduce biases and affect the accuracy of the model's predictions. However, soil degradation, due to loss of soil carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) pools, is declining the productivity of RRS and threatening the region’s food security. Intensive tillage along with improper residues and nutrient management practices are among the reasons of the loss of soil C and N pools and decline in rice productivity. The resource rich North Eastern region (NER) of India located in eastern Himalayas has a population of ∼47 million on a geographical area of 26.2 M ha (Das et al., 2015). The NER is characterized by di- versified agro- climatic conditions and topography (hills and valley), and about 70% of the region is hilly (Yadav et al., 2013a; Meena and Yadav, 2014). The plain areas and valleys surrounded by hills are used for rice cultivation (Das et al., 2014). Rice is a staple food of the NER, and is cultivated on about 3.5 Mha, which account for almost 8% of the land area and 6.5% of the country’s rice production (Choudhary et al., 2016). The RRS is the most pre-dominant system in the region (Yadav et al., 2013a). The major concern is that, despite the favorable edaphic and climatic conditions; the rice yield in the region hardly exceeds 2 Mg ha−1 as against national average of 2.8 Mg ha−1 in India and 4.42 Mg ha−1 in neighboring Bangladesh (Das et al., 2015). Food se- curity in the NER entirely depends on rice because no other cereals are grown by the farmers due to food habits and agro-climatic situations

knowledge.evidence: (Das et al., 2014; Yadav et al., 2017). Thus, self- sufficiency in food grains in the region can be achieved only through enhancement in productivity of RRS (Das et al., 2015). This is possible by developing improved resource- effective technologies, and management and re- storing soil’s C and N pools. The CA technologies with some mod- ification [e.g., RT, NT, INM (integrated nutrient management), use of micro nutrient, and residue retention] in rice–wheat and maize–wheat cropping system have been proven to increase productivity and the soil health under irrigated conditions in the Indo-Gangetic Plains (Singh et al., 2016). However, the research information on the impact of CA on productivity and sustainability of RRS under the rain-fed NER ecosys- tems is scanty (Nagarajan et al., 2013). Therefore, the present study was conducted to assess the effects of different tillage, nutrient and residue management options on system productivity, soil C and N pools of RRS under the climatic conditions of the NER of India. The experiment tested the hypothesis that conservation tillage with judicious manage- ment of nutrient and crop residues enhances the system productivity, and increases C and N sequestration in soils under RRS.

However, the need of irrigation of crop was based on the soil moisture content and weather conditions. The DR plots were kept flooded (5 cm of standing water) for the first 2 weeks, followed by irrigation (5 cm depth) at the appearance of cracks on the soil surface till maturity. On average, total irrigation water used in DR ranged between 800 and 900 ha-mm across the treatments. However, the highest amount of irrigation water was required under CT (900 ha- mm), because puddling consumed 200 ha-mm water. In contrast, the lowest amount was required under NT plots (800 ha-mm) due to retention of rice residues on the soil surface. Irrigation water to rice in different treatments was applied at all the critical growth stages so that crops were not affected by moisture stress.

The SOC was assumed to be equal to the total C with negligible inorganic C concentrations as the soil pH was below 7 (Jagadamma and Lal, 2010). Puddling increases soil ρb immediately below the plow layer due to destruction of soil aggregates, reduction in porosity by filling of macro- pores with finer soil particles, and the direct physical compaction caused by the tillage implements (Sharma et al., 2003; Gathala et al., 2011). The data presented herein suggest that RT in both WR and DR crops may have relatively positive effect on soil ρb. In contrast, other studies have reported higher ρb under NT at 0–5 cm depth compared to that under CT in cropping systems other than RRS (Gathala et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2012; Jat et al., 2013). Management- induced changes in soil ρb depend on texture, SOM content, tillage type and intensity, and cropping system (Sharma et al., 2003; Kharub et al., 2004). Any change in soil ρb in the present study may have been masked by its clay loam texture and the fact that soil samples were obtained from the middle of 0–20 cm upper layer. Soil sampling at smaller depth increments should be preferred to detect ρb variability in the surface layer.

The accumulation of crop residues on the soil surface is due to the enrichment of SOM in the surface layer and relatively higher mi- crobial activity in soil under NT and RT (Mathew et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2017). The concentration of SMBC is indicative of the soil's ability to store and cycle nutrients and SOM (Dick, 1992), and it also plays an im- portant role in physical stabilization of aggregates (Franzluebbers et al., 1999). Consequently, SMBC is an important indicator of soil quality, and is also closely related to soil fertility (Das et al., 2014). The rate of biomass-C input from plant residues is a predominant factor controlling the amount of SMBC (Campbell et al., 1997). The continuous and a uniform supply of biomass-C is an energy source for microorganisms (Das et al., 2014). Thus, RT/NT with INM and crop residues are ne- cessary for improving soil quality particularly in the depleted soils of NEH region (Boulal et al., 2008).

On average, active and passive carbon pools, TOC, and WBC stocks followed the order: S4 > S3 > S2 > S1 at all sites, except Gazipur, where the order was S3 > S4 > S2 > S1. CA practices stabilized applied carbon inputs to soil organic carbon at an annual rate of 1.7 %, with greater stabilization observed under S4 (11.7 %) > S3 (10.6 %) > S2 (7.8 %), regardless of location. Rice-rice sites exhibited a higher carbon stabilization rate (13.4 %) compared to rice- wheat sites (6.7 %). A significant proportion of stabilized carbon (63 %) was allocated to passive pools in soils under S2, S3, and S4, highlighting CA’s potential to enhance carbon stability. Using a linear indexing technique, we identified that both S3 and S4 are conducive to better carbon stabilization, yield sustainability, and envi- ronmental co-benefits. Consequently, full CA systems with best management practices (S3) and best management practices with crop diversification (S4) are recommended for sustainable crop production in the major double cereal growing regions of South Asia, including India and Bangladesh.

knowledge.evidence: 2.3.5. Optimization of the management practices We made an attempt to evaluate the relative performance of the CA- based management practices in different locations. The performance of the scenarios was assessed using linear indexing technique for the goodness of the system (Liebig et al., 2001). To this end, firstly the at- tributes/parameters were separated into two groups: one is the gain- parameters for which ‘more is better’, and it includes rice equivalent yield (REY), total organic carbon stabilized (%) and % passive carbon to TOC. The other is the loss-parameters for which ‘less is better’, and in- cludes global warming potential intensity (GWPi), energy input (EI). Values measured for each of the gain-parameters for the four scenarios were divided by its highest observed value so that the scenario with the highest value received a score between zero to one (Eq. (7)). Contrarily, values measured for each of the loss-parameters of the scenario were divided by its lowest observed value and made reciprocal so that the lowest observed value received a score between zero to one (Eq. (8)). Following such scoring for each of the parameters for all the scenarios, we summed up the scores and ranked the scenarios.

knowledge.evidence: The study revealed a positive response of total organic carbon (TOC) and Walkley-Black carbon (WBC) pools across various agroecological zones in South Asia to conservation agriculture (CA) practices, demon- strating a consistent increase compared to conventional agriculture methods. Both active and passive carbon pools exhibited increment under CA practices, indicating enhanced microbial activity, improved nutrient cycling, and increased soil carbon sequestration. Systems implementing full CA with best management practices (BMPs) (S3) and BMPs combined with crop diversification (S4) displayed favourable characteristics for carbon economy, including balanced carbon distri- bution (reflected in higher Carbon Management Index - CMI), increased carbon stocks, and greater carbon stabilization, particularly within passive pools. This trend contributes to the resilience and sustainability of agricultural systems, fostering higher crop productivity (reflected in higher Resource Use Efficiency - REY) while also delivering environ- mental co-benefits, such as reduced Global Warming Potential intensity (GWPi) and energy consumption. Consequently, these practices are recommended for wider adoption and promotion in the studied regions,

knowledge.evidence: The availability and spatial variability of soil nutrients strongly influence ecosystem services, food production, and sustainable land management, yet major information gaps persist at national and global scales. This study developed the first national digital maps of soil properties and nutrients for Mexico, contributing to the FAO's Global Soil Nutrient and Nutrient Budget Map (GSNmap) initiative. Using approximately 7000 harmonized soil observations at 0–30 cm depth and a comprehensive set of environmental covariates, we applied Quantile Regression Forest (QRF) models to predict soil texture (sand, silt, and clay contents), bulk density (BD), pH, cation exchange capacity (CEC), organic carbon (OC) and total nitrogen (N) contents, available phosphorus (P), and exchangeable potassium (K) and calcium (Ca) concentrations at 250 m resolution. Model performance was heterogeneous but overall robust at the national scale. Soil texture fractions, pH, CEC, OC, K, and Ca were predicted with moderate to strong accuracy (R2 ≈0.50–0.77). In contrast, N and P exhibited lower predictive accuracy (R2 ≤0.26), reflecting their strong sensitivity to localized management practices and land-use history,

DSM is a computer-assisted branch of soil cartography. On DSM, soil hard data (i.e., expensive, time consuming) is coupled in the statistical space with proxies of soil forming factors to predict soil property or class values across an entire area of interest (McBratney et al., 2003; Hengl, 2003; Scull et al., 2003). Using remote sensing, digital terrain analysis and statistical learning (e.g., geostatistics, ma­ chine learning) DSM has become the most cost-effective approach to characterize the spatial variability of soil property values or classes across scales. Integration of DSM with local expertise is particularly appealing for soil nutrient modeling and mapping. Soil nutrient availability depends on factors such as organic matter, texture, cation exchange capacity (CEC), and pH (Van Sundert et al., 2020). To capture this variability, the FAO's GSNmap initiative pro­ motes DSM to harmonize data and generate spatially explicit nutrient information (FAO, 2022a). QRF is a variant of Random Forests (RF)—a popular ensemble of regression trees based on bagging—(Breiman, 2001), which is a well known machine learning algorithm due its relatively high performance compared to other prediction algorithms on DSM (Vaysse and Lagacherie, 2017; Guevara et al., 2018). Consequently, the use of this algorithm represents a competitive statistical benchmark for wall- to-wall DSM mapping efforts in Mexico. knowledge.evidence: 2.1.1. Geographic and biophysical context This study was conducted at the national scale, encompassing all agricultural and grassland systems in Mexico (Fig. 1). The country spans latitudes 14◦–32◦N, where the Nearctic and Neotropical biogeographic regions converge, resulting in highly diverse topographic, climatic, and ecological conditions (Barreras et al., 2023). Mexico harbors 28 of the 32 soil groups recognized by the IUSS (2015), making it one of the most pedodiverse countries globally. Shallow and weakly developed soils such as Leptosols, Regosols, and Calcisols cover more than half of the territory, while more fertile soils such as Phaeozems, Luvisols, and Vertisols account for roughly one-third. This broad pedodiversity creates both challenges and opportunities for DSM, as nutrient availability is strongly conditioned by local soil–landscape interactions.

Model calibration and prediction We first applied a Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) strategy with repeated cross-validation to optimize model parameters and identify the most informative predictors. In each iteration, RFE evaluates the effect of removing individual variables on prediction error, retaining those whose absence most increases model error as the most informative predictors. The predictive framework was based on the RF algorithm (Breiman, 2001), widely used in DSM for its robustness, non-parametric nature, and ability to capture non-linear relationships between soil properties and environmental covariates (Vaysse and Lagacherie, 2017). Comparative reviews highlight that RF consistently performs better or at least as well as alternative algorithms in DSM applications, providing higher predictive accuracy and stability across different soil properties and covariate sets (Lamichhane et al., 2019; Pouladi et al., 2023). RF builds an ensemble of regression trees using bootstrap samples and random subsets of predictors (Breiman, 1996); predictions are obtained as the ensemble average. Model performance was primarily evaluated using the coefficient of determination (R2), which describes the proportion of variance explained, and the root mean squared error (RMSE), which reflects the overall magnitude of prediction errors. ANOVA detected highly significant differ­ ences among states for most variables (p < 0.001), and Tukey-adjusted post-hoc comparisons confirmed clear contrasts for soil texture, pH, CEC, OC, N, available P, exchangeable K and Ca. In contrast, BD did not show statistically significant differences among states, indicating rela­ tively homogeneous values at this spatial scale aggregation level. Textural composition varies markedly among states, although most exhibit intermediate sand contents, typically ranging between ~37% and ~ 50% (Table 6). States in northern and north-central Mexico tend to show higher sand proportions (e.g., Baja California, Sonora, Tlaxcala, Zacatecas and Chihuahua), whereas lower sand contents are observed in southeastern states such as Tabasco, Campeche and Yucat´an. Silt con­ tents generally range from ~22% to ~28%, with higher values in Tabasco and Veracruz and lower values in the Yucat´an Peninsula states.

OC contents range from ~0.6–1.0% in arid northern states such as Baja California, Baja California Sur and Sonora to >2.2% in Yucat´an and Quintana Roo. knowledge.evidence: Overall, the state-level analysis reveals that much of the regional variability described in the previous section is preserved—and in some cases amplified—when examined at finer spatial resolution. States within the Yucat´an Peninsula consistently concentrate the highest values of clay content, CEC, OC, N, K and Ca, while simultaneously exhibiting low available P, highlighting a distinct nutrient imbalance at this scale. In contrast, many northern and north-central states combine coarser textures, lower organic matter contents and more variable nutrient levels. The lack of statistically significant differences in BD across states, despite strong contrasts in texture and OC contents, sug­ gests that this property is less sensitive to state-level aggregation and likely reflects finer-scale controls not captured at this resolution. Together, these patterns provide a quantitative basis for interpreting how regional geology, climate and land-use history interact to shape soil fertility gradients across Mexico.

knowledge.evidence: The results of this study emphasize the importance of understanding soil properties at regional and state levels to inform land management practices across Mexico. While many soil attributes are strongly influ­ enced by inherent soil-forming factors, management practices can sub­ stantially modify properties such as soil OC and pH, particularly in regions characterized by intensive or long-standing agricultural use. The pronounced variability observed across the Yucat´an Peninsula, Northern Mexico, and Central-South Mexico highlights the need for regionally tailored strategies to sustain soil health and agricultural productivity. In the Yucat´an Peninsula, the combination of high CEC, elevated OC and exchangeable Ca contents, moderately alkaline pH, and low P availability reflects a distinctive edaphic configuration associated with carbonate-dominated parent materials. The consistently high OC con­ tents observed in this region are likely driven by stabilization mecha­ nisms characteristic of carbonate-rich soils, including physical protection and organo–carbonate associations linked to secondary car­ bonates derived from limestone. Under predominantly rainfed conditions, soil fertility constraints in this region arise from limitations in nutrient retention, use efficiency, and system stability, rather than from severe nutrient depletion. Slightly acidic pH conditions observed in states such as Mexico City, Tlaxcala, and the State of Mexico reflect both intrinsic soil-forming processes associated with more weathered parent materials and long-term nutrient removal under rainfed management. These patterns are consistent with the dominance of weathered volcanic soils such as Andosols, Phaeozems, and Cambisols in the region, which are commonly characterized by acidic pH, elevated Al contents, and limited buffering capacity (Sotelo-Ruiz et al., 2021). At the regional scale, these conditions are associated with moderate to low CEC and relatively low Ca contents, indicating reduced chemical resilience and increased sus­ ceptibility to nutrient losses. Although average available P contents are intermediate to relatively high compared with other regions, soil acidity likely reduces P use efficiency through enhanced sorption to Fe and Al

knowledge.evidence: Our study provides the first national digital maps of soil properties and nutrients for Mexico generated from harmonized national soil ob­ servations and DSM methodologies within the framework of the FAO's GSNmap program. Unlike previous compilations, the maps deliver spatially continuous information at pixel level together with model- based uncertainty estimates, produced through locally calibrated modeling. This represents both a methodological and applied contri­ bution aligned with GSNmap, with direct relevance for soil management and policy-making in Mexico. Importantly, this approach helps bridge a critical information gap by connecting local management needs with the global challenge of nutrient imbalance (Richardson et al., 2023). The accuracy assessment indicates heterogeneous but overall robust predictive performance across soil properties and nutrients. Texture variables and soil pH were predicted with strong agreement, supporting high-confidence interpretation of national-scale gradients. Moderate-to- strong performance was obtained for CEC, OC, exchangeable K and Ca, while BD showed consistent predictions. In contrast, N and available P were the most difficult variables to predict. By providing spatially continuous predictions accompanied by model- based uncertainty estimates, the maps represent a substantial advance over previous point-based compilations and offer an operational foun­ dation for soil assessment at regional and national scales. The results demonstrate that soil fertility constraints in Mexico are not governed by a single national pattern, but instead emerge from distinct combinations of climate, soil chemical and physical properties, and land-use history. knowledge.evidence: Soil Security includes dimensions, soil capability, soil condition, soil capital, soil connectivity and soil codifi­ cation (the “five C’s”). This article provides a short review on how soil mapping, digital soil mapping and soil monitoring systems (SM, DSM and SMS) over large areas contribute to these five C’s at scales ranging from country to globe. Changes and the evolution in aims of SM, DSM and SMS were driven both by main issues related to policy priorities and associated advances in science and technology. This review shows that SM, DSM and SMS can provide the basis for assessing soil capability and condition over large areas, especially if we assume that capability mainly depends on rather stable soil attributes. Repeated DSM or SMS are appropriated tool to monitor changes in soil condition at these scales. They may even allow mapping changes in soil capability. However, broad-scale SM, DSM and SMS have not yet fully achieved the provision of information concerning the delivery of some soil functions and soil-based ecosystem services. Although significant progress in estimating the capital dimension of soil security has been achieved, there is need to progress monitoring changes in soil capital.

knowledge.evidence: At the birth of pedology, soil science and large areas soil mapping were obviously linked. The scientist considered to be the father of pedology (Vassili Dokuchaev) was originally a geographer and cartog­ rapher. It was by traveling through Russia and making thousands of observations that he demonstrated the climatic zonality of Russia’s soils. Vassili Dokuchaev was the first who produced soil maps at continental scales (Boulaine, 1983). Seventy-three years later, it was by exploring and mapping the soils of northern France that Marcel Jamagne high­ lighted one of the most famous chrono-sequences of the evolution of silty soils in temperate climates (Jamagne, 1973, 1978; Jamagne et al., 1984). Undoubtedly, the study of the spatial distribution of soils and their properties is a major tool for understanding their pedogenesis. However, recent developments in this field were rarely driven by the concern for the study of pedogenesis. The two main drivers of meth­ odological changes in broad-scale SM, DSM and SMS were related both to pressing societal issues that countries and policy-makers had to solve, and to scientific and technological advancements with time. knowledge.evidence: As defined by McBratney et al. (2014) and Field (2017) soil capability ”asks what this soil can do?”. This dimension implies that under a given climate and landscape, different types of soil, characterized by some biophysical properties, may perform different functions. Soil capability is thus mainly influenced by soil attributes that are considered as more or less stable except in case of drastic changes (e.g., landslide, severe erosion, sudden and high contamination, flooding). As such, capability is strongly linked to intrinsic soil characteristics. Most of the SM, DSM and SMS scheme ensure a strong link to these intrinsic soil characteristics. Conventional SM usually delineates soil classes on the basis of the suc­ cession of horizons that are supposed to have analog properties. If the delineation is accurate, and if the variability of soil types is well captured by the map, then we can make the hypothesis that, under the same climate, vegetation and topography, traditional soil maps may help to map soil capability. Placing monetary values on natural resources allows people to better understand their significance (McBratney et al., 2019a, 2019b). Soil is part of a natural capital defined as the “stock of materials of information contained within an ecosystem” (Costanza et al., 1997). The stocks contained within the soil include, for instance, SOC stocks, available water for plants, nutrients, material for building, areas avail­ able for different land uses. This capital, however, does not necessarily have to be converted into financial or market values. Related to the topic of our paper, ex­ amples of opinion papers and letters to the editor about the concepts of “Soil Quality”, “Soil Health”, and, unavoidably, now, “Soil Security” are numerous. These are scientific discussions and we do not blame them. New concepts do need to withstand thorough scientific debate prior to a general acceptance by the scientific community yet they should remain constructive. Moreover, exacerbating these debates outside of our community is counter-productive. A real question is “should we communicate only on what is scientifically defined and agreed”? We may have to wait for years. Who will decide that a concept is “scien­ tifically defined and agreed”? We are afraid that it is not a good practice for communication. Repeated DSM or SMS are appropriated tool to monitor changes in soil condition with time at these scales. In case of some drastic changes, they may even allow to map changes in soil capability. knowledge.evidence: evaluating the capital dimension Soil Security? We clearly show exam­ ples demonstrating that soil capital state and changes can be assessed by estimating quantities of soil and related elements, by evaluating the ecosystem services they render, or by transforming their capital or their services into monetary values. Although significant progress in esti­ mating the capital dimension of soil security has been achieved thanks to broad-scale SM, DSM and SMS, yet there is the need to progress moni­ toring changes in soil capital. Remote sensing offers a promising tool for this, but we must keep in mind that it cannot cover all the aspects of soil capital and that it is often limited to information related to land-use change, net primary productivity, or to topsoil properties. We must also keep in mind that soil capital may be perceived in different ways by different actors, and that our estimates of changes in soil capital should cover these different perceptions. How does the development of SM, DSM and SMS contribute to the soil connectivity? Does it enable an increase in soil connectivity and awareness, and to which target audiences? We show that there is a great potential of broad-scale SM, DSM and SMS to increase soil connectivity.

knowledge.evidence: Nitrogen (N) is an essential nutrient for crop growth, influencing both agricultural productivity and ecosystem processes. Conventional fertilizer recommendations often rely solely on soil N availability at sampling points, lacking information on its spatial variability. High-resolution spatial data are therefore crucial for sustaining sericulture production. This study represents the first effort to develop a spatial prediction map of available N in the Lakhimpur district, using 160 soil samples along with local environmental covariates. Five machine learning algorithms—Random Forest (RF), Cubist, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)—were employed to predict available N in the plough layer (0–15 cm) at a 30 m resolution. Measured N values ranged from 102 to 580 kg ha⁻¹. Under random cross-validation, RF consistently outperformed other models (R²c = 0.96, RMSEc = 40.69 kg ha⁻¹ in calibration and R²v = 0.35, RMSEv = 70.44 kg ha⁻¹ in validation). In contrast, spatial cross-validation resulted in markedly lower accuracy across all models, with R² values varied between 0.02 and 0.27. Recent advances in data science, the availability of high-resolution remote sensing imagery, and improved computational power have made it possible to incorporate a wide range of covariates—such as spectral indices, terrain derivatives, climate surfaces, and biological indicators—into predictive models. This integration significantly improves the accuracy of soil nitrogen pre­ dictions, especially in heterogeneous landscapes (Mponela et al. 2020; Zhou et al. 2020; Maleki et al. 2023). knowledge.evidence: Systematic randomised sampling was used to gather 160 composite samples of top soils (0–15 cm) from the Lakhimpur district of Assam. Using a v-notch technique, topsoil samples (0–15 cm) were gathered from the research area by systematic randomised sampling. The first cleaning was chosen at every test location to provide a soil sample free of debris. To capture every aspect of the field situation, 200 g of composite samples were created on the spot using the proportionate approach. Each composite sample is made up of ten individual samples. There was a 500g minimum quantity restriction on the replication. The laboratory received all of the composite replicates. After letting each duplicate air dry in the shade, they were sieved using a 2 mm sieve. Alkaline potas­ sium permanganate was used to calculate the available N (Subbiah and Asija, 1956).

knowledge.evidence: The SCORPAN model uses environmental characteristics, including climate (c), age (a), geographical position (n), organisms (o), parent material (p), and relief (r), to indirectly infer soil class/properties at a given location (McBratney et al. 2003). The SCORPAN model provides the quantitative (empirical) link between soil properties and factors that regulate spatial variability. The basic concept of the SCORPAN model lies in Dokuchaev (1976) and Jenny (1941) ideas. S = f(s, c,o, r, p, a, n) (1) The SCORPAN model may take in soil data through point data, spectral features (remotely sensed), or pre-existing soil maps. Environ­ mental variables are digitally and geographically explicit raster data processed by a geographic information system (GIS). Quantifying the relationships between spatially explicit digital environmental factors and the expected soil qualities is facilitated by the SCORPAN model. Uncertainty estimate is more straightforward when comparing the SCORPAN model to other conventional techniques.

knowledge.evidence: A total of twenty-eight environmental covariates (ECs), considered to be associated with pedogenesis, were compiled from multiple sources, including satellite-derived datasets and index products. These covariates were organized into major groups, namely climate, relief, parent ma­ terial, organisms, location, remote sensing, and soil-related factors. In digital soil mapping (DSM), data from the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager (OLI) have been extensively employed due to its 30 m spatial resolution and 16-day revisit cycle (Moharana et al. 2022). Surface reflectance products and associated vegetation indices were generated from the Landsat 8 Surface Reflectance Level-1 Tier 1 collection (USGS, accessed May 25, 2023). Among the spectral covariates, the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) along with reflectance data from all eleven Landsat bands were incorporated into the modeling framework to aid in predicting soil nitrogen (Table 1). Relief-based covariates were computed using a 30 m digital elevation model (DEM) derived from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM). Various terrain attributes were generated in SAGA-GIS version 6.3.0, including channel network base level (CNBL), convergence index (CI), channel network distance

Random forest The Random Forest (RF) algorithm operates on the principle of bi­ nary recursive partitioning and is constructed from an ensemble of Classification and Regression Trees (CART). Each tree in the ensemble is generated by repeatedly splitting the dataset into nodes based on pre­ dictor variables, thereby establishing relationships between explanatory and response variables. By aggregating the predictions of multiple trees, RF enhances model accuracy and reduces overfitting compared to single decision trees. Two parameters are particularly important in optimizing model performance: the number of trees to be grown in the forest (Ntree) and the number of predictor variables randomly sampled at each node split (Mtry). These parameters can be systematically tuned during the modeling process to achieve more robust and reliable predictive outcomes. The aggregate of the all-individual tree’s (algorithms) out­ comes is the ultimate forecast made by RF. Bootstrapping the original datasets achieves an Out-of-bag (OOB) estimation of error. This rule-based regression tree environment allows Cubist to capture both linear and non-linear patterns within soil–environmental covariate relationships.
