knowledge.evidence: Our study compares yield and irrigation water use in practice be­ tween puddled transplanted and direct-seeded rice – a water saving technology. To achieve this we quantified IWP and the factors driving it under the conventional PTR and DSR establishments using data from the farmers’ fields. The analysis highlights that higher IWP is achievable by adopting DSR compared to the conventional PTR practice. Although prior on-station experimental studies (research trials) have established similar findings (Alam et al., 2018; Yadav et al., 2011b, 2021), farmers practices remained poorly understood. Our results demonstrate that indeed a higher IWP within the range of 17.8 %–50.0 % can be obtained across the region for DSR farmers compared to PTR farmers – these are however less than in experimental station trials. The water saving in DSR is largely due to the accompanied adoptions of varities with shorter crop cycles and farmers irrigating with intermittent dry and wet cycles rather than constant flooding. Although we found some DSR farmers over-irrigate vis a vis crop requirements, much of the excess water is not lost and recharges aquifers through return flows. Additionally, reduced water use from DSR reduces on-farm energy consumption, with a scope

One of the most critical variables identified in the quantitative analysis to control the IWP especially under DSR establishment is date of sowing or transplanting. Overall, a lower IWA is found for the farms where late sowing (early June) is done compared to the early sowing (beginning of May). This is because the late sowing coincides with the monsoon onset which generally meets the crop water requirement and reduce evapotranspiration. This finding aligns with other studies (Singh et al., 2019; Urfels et al., 2022) and corroborated during the FGDs with farmers expressing awareness of the high water use associated with early sowing. But the majority of the DSR farmers continue sowing early to achieve profit maximization through triple cropping. This is illustrated by statements such as follows: I think the soil drinks more water if I sow on early May as it is dry and hot. This increases the number of irrigations; however, I need to cultivate three crops in a year, and I have no choice than early sowing. Peer influence, especially from older farmers, plays a crucial role in shaping farmers’ behaviors, as noted in studies by Johnson et al. (2023); Pathak et al. (2024) and Wang et al. It is crucial to note that beyond the plot-level factors such as sowing date, soil moisture, well depth and density, and education level, broader institutional and behavioral drivers also shape the irrigation practices across these two districts. In particular, free electricity in farms en­ courages farmers to apply water beyond crop requirements (Fishman et al., 2015; Shah, 2009) facilitating groundwater pumping. Limited access to effective extension services and decision-support tool further compounds this tendency, as many farmers instead rely on traditional knowledge or peer practices that favor risk-averse strategies, including over-irrigation as a safeguard against rainfall variability and potential disruptions due to power cuts (Kaur et al., 2021). While a detailed quantitative analysis of these drivers is beyond the scope of the present study, acknowledging these factors helps contextualize why farmers’ actual IWA is observed to be 1.6–2 folds higher than the experimental trials. Addressing these structural and behavioral influences through policy reform, targeted training, and improved advisory services could compliment technical interventions to promote more efficient water use

Splitting farms into smaller sub-plots Literature reveals inconsistencies in reporting the average land­ holding size in Haryana, which typically ranges between 2.2 ha (5.4 ac) and 4.5 ha (11.3 ac) (Ajay et al., 2022). Regardless of the total land­ holding, farmers often divide their fields into 0.4 ha (1 ac) plots for easier management (Waha et al., 2020). During irrigation, pumps are operated continuously until each plot is completely watered. However, frequent power outages and split 8-h power supply into shifts often result in re-irrigation. To avoid this, some farmers advocate for dividing the plots into smaller units of 0.2 ha (0.5 ac) with added benefit of uniform water distribution across the plots. One of the farmers reported: The frequency of power cuts in my village has intensified over the last two years. This has led to reirrigation on the same block (sub- plot) as the water does not reach the tail end during the first split of power supply. Therefore, I have divided each block into 0.5 acres (~0.2 ha) and have made channels in the periphery of my plots for uninterrupted water flow to other sub-plots. Now the power cuts do not induce any re-irrigation of my sub-plots.

Tar-wattar DSR Tar-wattar (delayed irrigation) DSR involves direct seeding under optimal soil moisture (or at field capacity), typically achieved by irri­ gating the field after land preparation and a few days prior to sowing (Yadav et al., 2013). Water is saved in this establishment since the subsequent irrigation is generally done 7–21 days after sowing, thus reducing 3–4 consecutive irrigations. This practice is generally not performed by the Haryanvi farmers, who prefer dry DSR over the tar-wattar DSR. In addition, weed pressure can be higher under Tar-wattar DSR and needs to be carefully managed. Studies have demonstrated that a delay in 21 days in the first irrigation post sowing had insignificant effect on rice yield, however, an overall reduction of 17.1 % in IWA (Kaur et al., 2024). This is because under conventional DSR practice, sowing is done in the first to second week of May when the crop water demand is at peak and with postponing the first irrigation up to 21 days can significantly reduce the overall IWA. Additionally, the succeeding water demand is met by the monsoon, reducing the irriga­ tion requirements.

knowledge.evidence: IWP is a vital indicator with the potential to restore groundwater reserves in northwest India if effectively monitored. It is influenced by multiple drivers, and identifying these is essential for implementing sustainable policies and agronomic practices to enhance IWP. This is the first study in which we measured and reported IWA and IWP from farmers’ fields at a landscape scale. We deployed 100 water flowmeters, evenly distributed between DSR and PTR farms across two rice- dominated districts in Haryana. We monitored seasonal IWA and calculated the IWP for 2023 and 2024 under both cultivation methods. Following this, we employed a mixed-method analysis incorporating variables such as biophysical characteristics, climate, farming practices, and demography, to identify key factors influencing IWP. Our findings suggest that, overall DSR farmers use less irrigation water than PTR farmers – but large variability exists within DSR farmers due to differ­ ences in antecedent soil moisture, and sowing dates. Additionally, power availability is crucial for affecting water use of all farmers. Furthermore, our results also suggest that the introduction of short-duration rice va­ rieties with DSR is accompanied by a shift in farmers’ cropping practice

knowledge.evidence: As developed by Professor J.A. Allan, the concept of ‘virtual water’ has been introduced for water-short countries in recent years. These countries can minimize their use of water and achieve food security at the same time by importing a portion of their food requirements from other areas or countries where water resources are adequate and available at a lower cost (Allan, 1996). Trading of other water-intensive commodities such as hydro-electric power falls in the domain of this concept in a similar way. The nations receiving food and electric power not only get the commodities but also the water that is necessary to produce them. Since this water is ‘virtually’ embedded in the commodity, it is called ‘virtual water’ (Allan, 1999a). 168 M. Qadir et al. / Agricultural Water Management 62 (2003) 165–185

knowledge.evidence: The concept of virtual water compares the amount of water embodied in a crop that can be purchased internationally with the amount of water which would be required to produce that crop domestically. For instance, for every kilogram of wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) imported, the water-stressed country will also get about 1 m3 (1000 l) of virtual water at much less cost than the price or value of the same quantity of water from the local water resources, if available, in the country itself (Allan, 1999b). This means that import of each megagram (1 Mg = 1 tonne) of wheat grain has about 1000 m3 (1000 Mg) of virtual water embedded in it. Similar calculations can be made for other food items requiring greater amounts of water in the production process (Table 1). It is, therefore, easier and less ecolog- ically destructive to import grain rather than to pipe 1000 times greater amount of water to produce the same commodity (Turton, 1999). The nations with scarce water resources gain by importing water-intensive commodities, while exporting goods that require less water in production. This strategy is particularly important in years when the world prices of food commodities are lower than the cost of production in water-stressed areas (Wichelns, 2001).

knowledge.evidence: in a manner that does not adversely affect the growing crops. This will prevent excessive accumulation of salts in the root zone. The extra quantity of irrigation water, referred to as leaching requirement, must be able to pass through the root zone. Adequate drainage is an essentiality for obtaining a desired leaching requirement to maintain soil salinity at levels suitable for crop growth. It also keeps the water table sufficiently deep to permit adequate root development, prevents the net upward flow of salt-laden groundwater into the root zone, and permits the movement and operations of farm implements in the fields (Shalhevet, 1994; Rhoades, 1999). Artificial drainage systems must be installed if adequate natural drainage is not available. The re-use of saline and saline-sodic drainage waters, which may be feasible based on research and farmers’ experiences, would reduce its volume. Minimizing the volume of irri- gation water applied in the first place would also reduce the drainage volume and minimize the leaching fraction. Minimizing the leaching fraction (1) maximizes the precipitation of applied Ca2+, HCO3−, and SO42−salts as calcite and gypsum in the soil, and (2) min- imizes the pickup of weathered and dissolved salts from the soil (Rhoades et al., 1974).

Blending consists of mixing good- and poor-quality water supplies before or during ir- rigation. A prerequisite for blending is a controlled way of mixing both the water supplies. Blending results in greater surface soil salinity over time, which af- fects seedling establishment and crop yield, and so less opportunity to grow high economic value salt-sensitive crops. However, this strategy may be more practical for situations where drainage water or shallow groundwater is not too saline for the crops. The sequential strategy involves applying the relatively better quality water to the crop with a lower salt resistance, then using the drainage water from that field – obtained through a tile drainage system – to irrigate crops that have the capability to withstand greater con- centrations of salts. The simplest management method is to sequentially use drainage water on fields located down-slope from those where the drainage water is collected. There is no fixed number of times for which a drainage water may be sequentially used. Such usage depends on the salinity, sodicity, and concentration of toxic minor elements in the drainage water, volume of water available, and the economic value and acceptable yield of the crop to be grown with the water. The long-term feasibility of drainage water re-use for irrigation would likely be increased if implemented on a regional scale rather than on a farm scale.

knowledge.evidence: Grattan and Rhoades (1990) have provided a schematic presentation of regional drainage water re-use strategy. Regional management of drainage water permits its re-use in ded- icated areas so as to localize the impacts of its use while other areas, such as up-slope areas, can be irrigated solely with better quality water. The second-generation drainage water from the primary re-use area may be discharged to other dedicated re-use areas where even more salt-resistant crops can be grown successfully. Ideally, regional coordination and cost-sharing among growers should be undertaken in such a re-use system. The anticipated future scenario of good-quality water shortage suggests that the time has come for the appropriate management of poor-quality water resources, i.e. to inter- cept, isolate, and re-use drainage waters within the regions where they are generated. The suitability of drainage waters for irrigation depends very much on the relative need and economic and environmental benefits that can be derived compared to other alternatives and on the specific conditions of use. A crucial management decision before implementing the re-use of drainage water is selection of a suitable plant species (Table 4). Production

If a livestock production system is based on the re-use of drainage water, it can transform such drainage waters from an environmental burden into an economic asset. These production systems can reduce the amount of water that must be disposed off and provide the incentive to install needed artificial drainage systems to sustain and improve soil quality. knowledge.evidence: Being so fundamental to the social, economic, and environmental sustainability of dif- ferent regions, water is a strategic resource particularly for water-starved countries where more than 40% of the present global population lives. Owing to the use of different criteria, there has been a skepticism concerning potential availability of water for food production to meet the future needs of the expanding population. However, there should be no anxiety in any region of the world, including Middle East and Africa, about the availability of water for drinking and domestic use and for almost all industrial and service sector uses. These sectors hardly use 25% of the freshwater resources. Agriculture is the largest single user of water with about 75% of freshwater being used for irrigation. Whenever the demand for freshwater increases a competition among municipal, industrial, and agricultural sectors often ends up in a decreased allocation to agriculture. We believe that the following strategies may serve as the essential components of sustainable agricultural water management in such countries: (1) potential use of ‘virtual water’ as a global solution to regional deficits, (2) improvement in current efficiencies of agricultural water use and conservation, (3) development of economically and environmentally accept- able methods for protection and improvement of water and soil quality, and (4) re-use of saline and/or sodic waters in certain dedicated areas. Since there is no single way to cope with the freshwater shortage, suitable combinations of these strategies will help resolve the water crisis, or at least will decrease its intensity in water-starved countries.

knowledge.evidence: The Northwest India (States of Punjab and Haryana) is one of the most important agricultural regions in the country as it contributes about 52% in nations food production (Abrol, 1999). Rice–wheat cropping sequence is the major food production system in the region, which earlier supported upland crops like maize, cotton and sorghum during kharif/ summer (June–October) and wheat during rabi/winter (November–April) seasons. The introduction of rice crop was largely a consequence of waterlogging in canal irrigated areas and development of an intensive network of shallow tubewells. The cultivation of wheat is practiced in about 80% of the area, which even includes marginal quality groundwater areas, mainly due to its low water requirement, tolerance to salinity and consistent market demand resulting in an assured return (Tyagi et al., 2005). Therefore, the rice– wheat cropping sequence in the region evolved due to specific regional climatic and geo-hydrological conditions. Although, the average productivity in the Northwest India is one of the highest in the country (7–8 Mg/ha for the rice–wheat sequence), there are considerable crop yield differences within this region (Ambast et al., 2004a).

knowledge.evidence: The study investigates the possibility of enhancing crop water productivity in the parts of Northwest India where groundwater quality is marginal and canal water supply is severely scarce. Soil, Water, Atmosphere and Plant (SWAP) model was calibrated and validated in three farmers’ fields with varying canal water availability and groundwater quality in the Kaithal Irrigation Circle of the Bhakra Canal system, Haryana. On the basis of predicted and observed soil water content, pressure heads, salt concentration at 2 week intervals and crop yields, the model was found suitable for use in the region. A few nomographs were prepared to provide a graphical method to predict the effect of different combinations of water quality and depth of water application on crop yield and soil salinity and to help develop some guidelines to the farming community. Water management alternatives at the field level were suggested to increase the yield and to maintain soil salinity below threshold level. The application of frequent irrigation in precisely leveled field would help in achieving 10% higher yield even when saline groundwater of 11 dS/m is used for irrigation. # 2008 Elsevier B.V. Irrigation of 10 cm additional water than the normally practiced 25 cm of water application in farmer’s fields will increase the pumping cost by 810 INR/ha (pumping cost is taken at 0.81 INR/m3 for diesel operated pumps; Tyagi et al., 2005) but will give an additional average income of 5000 INR/ha (1 US$ = 45 INR). Further, crop choices for an area can be made depending upon the quantity and quality of available irrigation water. knowledge.evidence: good quality water (EC = 1 dS/m) one can get a relative yield of 0.86 that may reduce to 0.4, if salinity of water increases to 11 dS/m. Laser land leveller helps in achieving precision land leveling (leveling index <1.5 cm) and thus provides the scope of applying shallow depth (4 cm) of irrigation water more frequently (Ambast et al., 2004b). Irrigation scheduling with application of 4 cm water was considered as an improvement option and its effect on crop yield was simulated. It has been observed that relative yield increased from 0.86 to 0.92 with eight irrigations (4 cm) of good quality water (EC < 1 dS/m). After eight irrigations no significant increase in the yield has been observed. In case of 11 dS/m water, the relative yield increased significantly higher (from 0.45 to 0.60) due to frequent irrigation as compared to good quality water. The increase in relative yield has been seen as a result of frequent irrigations that reduced the salinity build up in the root zone depth before it reaches to threshold level. Even the minimum increase in yield (360 kg/ha) alone ensures the net return of 2400 INR/ha (apart from saving money due to reduced pumping time), which offsets the cost of laser land levelling

knowledge.evidence: In the arid and semi-arid regions, where canal water availability is scarce and groundwater quality is marginally saline, conjunctive use of waters is quite common. Lack of understanding of interaction of different combinations of water quantity and quality on crop yield and soil salinity prohibits the scope for suggesting possible options of improving land and water productivity. In this paper, SWAP model has been calibrated and validated in the Kaithal irrigation circle, Haryana in the Northwest India. It has been observed that model simulates, with sufficient accuracy, the observed field values on soil moisture content, pressure head, soil salinity and crop yield and thus could be used for developing different scenarios of conjunctive water use of canal and ground water. Initially an attempt has been made to analyze the impact of various combinations of water quantity and quality on crop yield and soil salinity. Further, a few nomographs depicting effect of different combinations of waters on crop yield and soil salinity have been developed as ready reference for farmers decision making. knowledge.evidence: The authors of the recently completed Comprehensive Assessment of Water Management in Agriculture (CA) concluded that there are sufficient water resources to produce food for a growing population but that trends in consumption, production and environmental patterns, if continued, will lead to water crises in many parts of the world. Only if we act to improve water use will we meet the acute fresh water challenge. Recent spikes in food prices, partially caused by the increasing demand for agricultural products in non-food uses, underline the urgent need to invest in agricultural production, of which water management is a crucial part. The world experienced similar pressure on per capita food supplies and food prices in the 1960s and 1970s, but the challenges now are different than those we experienced 50 years ago. The world’s population is substantially larger, there are many more people living in poverty, and the costs of many agricultural inputs are much higher. knowledge.evidence: Fluctuating energy prices impact agriculture, and thus, agricultural water management, in different ways. First, as the demand for alternative energy sources, including hydropower and energy from biomass increases, so does the demand for water; with implications also for water allocation among competing sectors. Second, the cost of pumping groundwater, a major input in agricultural production around the world, increases. Third, when energy prices increase, the viability of desalinization as a source of water for irrigation and other uses declines. Finally, fertilizer prices and the unit costs of other petroleum-based inputs rise with increases in energy prices. At present the contribution of biofuels to the world’s energy supply is very modest, but might increase as a result of rising energy prices, geopolitics, and public concerns regarding the impacts of greenhouse gas emissions. This potentially leads to more intensive competition for land and water resources between food and fuel, particularly where energy demand is high and water is scarce, such as in India and China (De Fraiture et al., 2008). Recent increases in global food prices are due partially to increased production of biofuels (Von Braun, 2008).

knowledge.evidence: Water scarcity is a critical constraint to agriculture in many parts of the world. Physical water scarcity occurs when available water resources are insufficient to meet all demands, including environ- mental flow requirements. Economic water scarcity occurs when investments needed to maintain pace with growing water demand are constrained by financial, human, or institutional capacity (Seckler et al., 1998). Today an estimated 1.2 billion people live in river basins characterized by physical scarcity and another 1.5 billion live in economically scarce basins (Molden et al., 2007). With increasing water demands, these numbers are expected to increase. Limited water endowments are an obvious cause of physical water scarcity. Inadequate investments in water storage and management are typical causes of economic water scarcity. Millions of poor, small-scale farmers operate in conditions of either physical or economic water scarcity. In many arid and semi- arid areas, investments and policies are needed to improve farm- level access to irrigation water and enhance agricultural produc- tivity. Even in some humid areas, new investments and policies are needed to ensure that water resources are allocated and used

knowledge.evidence: Rainwater harvesting (RWH), the small-scale collection and storage of runoff to augment groundwater stores, has been seen as a solution to the deepening groundwater crisis in India. However, hydrological impacts of RWH in India are not well understood, particularly at the larger catchment-scale. A key element to grasping RWH impact involves understanding the generated recharge variability in time and space, which is the result of variability in rainfall-runoff and efficiency of RWH structures. Yet there are very few reported empirical studies of the impact of RWH. Catchment-scale impacts are best studied using a water balance model, which would require a basic level of field data and understanding of the variability. This study reports the results of a 2-year field study in the 476 km2 semi-arid Arvari River catchment, where over 366 RWH structures have been built since 1985. Difficulties associated with working in semi- arid regions include data scarcity. Potential recharge estimates from seven RWH storages, across three different types and in six landscape positions, were calculated using the water balance method. knowledge.evidence: the water table fluctuation method. The average daily potential recharge from RWH structures varied between 12 and 52 mm/day, while estimated actual recharge reaching the groundwater ranged from 3 to 7 mm/day. The large difference between recharge estimates could be explained through soil storage, local groundwater mounding beneath structures and a large lateral transmissivity in the aquifer. Overall, approximately 7% of rainfall is recharged by RWH in the catchment, which was similar in the compara- tively wet and dry years of the field analysis. There were key differences between RWH structures, due to engineering design and location. These results indicate that recharge from RWH affects the local ground- water table, but also has potential to move laterally and impact surrounding areas. However, the greatest weakness in such analysis is the lack of information available on aquifer characteristics, in addition to geology and soil type. © 2010 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

Rainwater harvesting gener- ally results in increased crop production and greater crop yield, because resulting rises in the water table mean better accessibility and yields of groundwater (Keller et al., 2000). The ‘groundwater recharge movement’ in India has been promoting and reinvesting in RWH over the past three decades (Sakthivadivel, 2007, 2008). Until recently, RWH was seen as a totally benign technology, as the impact of an individual dam was considered relatively small (Batchelor et al., 2003). This despite the fact that the cumulative impact of RWH structures on stream flows could be significant (Calder et al., 2006). Rainwater harvesting redistributes the available water resources across the catchment, by increasing the annual amount of catch- ment rainfall that becomes stored recharge, which changes other water balance components, including evaporation and stream flow. The arguments against RWH have not yet been confirmed by any empirical studies. This is because the few empirical studies in India have focussed largely on local-scale RWH impacts and have not considered larger catchment hydrological impacts, or the surface water–groundwater interactions (Badiger et al., 2002; Gontia and Sikarwar, 2005; Neumann et al., 2004; Sharda et al., 2006). In the catchment there has been significant reinvestment in RWH over the last 20 years, which is the result of the work of the community and a local non-government organisation (NGO), Tarun Bharat Sangh. As a result, this makes it an interesting case study to evaluate the impacts of RWH on a larger scale. How- ever, as is typical for many semi-arid catchments, the catchment is ungauged and there is no climate station within the catch- ment. knowledge.evidence: The climate is semi-arid with hot summers between March and June. May and June are the hottest months of the year with a mean daily maximum and minimum temperature in May of 42.1 and 25.7 ◦C. The winter extends from November to March, with temper- atures dropping to an average minimum of 7.7 ◦C and an average maximum of 21 ◦C in January. Eighty percent of the rainfall falls during the south-westerly monsoon between June and September. The closest rainfall station to the Arvari River catchment is in the nearby town of Thanagazi (15 km to the North of the catchment), which has an average yearly rainfall of 705.8 mm. Each year there is an average of 8 rainfall days greater than 35 mm with an average of 31 rainy days a year (1901–2002). Total annual potential evapo- transpiration is 1523.7 mm, highest in May (271.5 mm/month) and lowest in December (155.6 mm/month).

In the greater Banganga River Basin, groundwa- ter occurs in shallow alluvium layers and deeper hard rock areas. The sandy and coarse sediments of the alluvial system overly the fractured igneous and metamorphic hard rock aquifers, and is con- nected hydraulically (Gale et al., 2002). Examined soil profiles in the catchment were dominated by a shallow, well-drained, loamy skeletal soil, which is severely eroded and strongly stony. Saprolite is commonly seen throughout the catchment and bedrock is reached at shallow depths. Land use reflects soil type, with agriculture found on the alluvial deeper clay soils, while forest areas were on the slopes on shallower soils. There is limited small-scale information about geological and soil characteristics in this catchment.

knowledge.evidence: Six villages in the middle and upper reaches of the Arvari catchment were identified for detailed studies of wells and RWH structures over 2007 and 2008, based on position and accessibil- ity. These focus areas are located mainly in the middle and upper reaches of the catchment (Fig. 1, Table 2). In each focus area a RWH structure was monitored, along with dug wells in the vicinity of the structure (Table 2). In Bhaonta, two cascading Bandhs were monitored, in Lalpura and Jhiri earthen Johads were monitored, and finally in Hamirpur, Nitata and Kaled Anicuts that lie across the main reach of the river were observed. As there are no official instrumented piezometers in the catchment, groundwater levels in 29 dug wells were monitored throughout 2007 and 2008. Three rain gauges were set up in Bhaonta, Hamirpur and Sirinagar to collect daily rainfall (Fig. 1).

The noise in the data, as indicated by the root mean square error (RMSE) and the standard deviation (Table 4), is a reflection of the difficulties associated with estimating the planar surface area of the structures, which had highly irregular shapes. Total volume of Rep was greatest at Sankara Bandh (Fig. 5a). knowledge.evidence: Potential recharge was converted from m3/day to mm/day by dividing by the average surface area of the structures. The average daily Rep rates (mm/day) (Table 5) in 2008 are much greater than in 2007, as more rainfall in 2008 meant more stored water in the RWH storage areas. The rate of potential recharge depends on the shape and size of the structure storage area, runoff characteristics (local rainfall and land cover), and infiltration characteristics in the storage area (soil depth and underlying bed rock). In the Johads, the soil depth was deeper and had higher clay content compared to the Bandhs, which would influence the infiltration capacity of the stored water. For all structures the total volume of Rep increases as the rainfall increases. As only 2 years of field data has been col- lected, it is difficult to determine the exact relationship between annual rainfall and annual recharge. However, the observed data indicate the range of Rep values that can occur across a variable landscape. The type of structure determines the range of potential recharge values. This can probably be explained by the fact that the structures types were purpose built to fulfil different objectives, which results in similar properties across the catchment.

knowledge.evidence: As discussed in Section 3, discharge across three Anicuts that lie across the main reach of the river was also monitored. In 2007, the Anicut at Hamirpur overflowed on 8 days towards Kaled. At Kaled Anicut, overflow occurred for 22 days and further downstream towards Sainthal Sagar dam, at Sirinagar, there was no stream flow (see Fig. 1 for catchment position). On the other tributary, at Nitata, the Anicut overflowed on 6 days. In 2008, the increased rainfall led to more flow; Hamirpur 24 days, Nitata 11 days, but Kaled had the longest overflow, flowing daily through the months of July to early November. The peaks occurred in all the Anicuts at similar times, mostly when large rainfall events occurred and therefore greater runoff events reached the river. knowledge.evidence: The wells at Bhaonta saw a greater response in groundwater level in 2008 than in 2007 (Fig. 7a and b), due to less pumping and more rainfall in 2008. The relative responses in 2008 of BK1, BK2, BK4 and BK5 wells show a greater increase than in BK3 and BK6 (Fig. 7b), which could be attributed to their landscape positions. Wells BK3 and BK6 are in a valley that runs parallel to the valley within which the Bandhs are found, so recharge may take longer to reach these wells due to differences in hydrogeology. Well BK5 was the shallowest well, close to the surface in a fractured rock area, while BK1 and BK2 were in the agriculture land and thus in alluvial deposits. The response from well BK5 closely mirrored the RWH structures water storage patterns of rise and fall (Fig. 7c), high- lighting the direct influence of recharge from RWH on groundwater levels. Wells BK4 and BK 6 are almost 1 km away from Sankara Bandh and 600 m from Beruji Bandh, but the influence of recharge on groundwater levels in these wells can still be clearly seen. This could be the result of large lateral transmissivity as Bhaonta is in a higher rocky elevation area and there are larger volumes of Rep coming from the Bandhs, particularly from Sankara Bandh.

The rainfall at Hamir- pur was used to calculate the percentage of rainfall that becomes recharge from the similar sized Anicuts/Bandhs and Johads/Talab in the catchment (Table 10) at the catchment scale. In 2007 around 6.6% of rainfall became Rep, and in 2008 about 7%. These values are actually quite similar to recharge efficiency estimates from the monitored RWH structures (Table 7). knowledge.evidence: A key question in relation to rainwater harvesting (RWH) is whether the technique increases the sustain- ability of irrigated agriculture. A conceptual water balance model, based on field data from the Arvari River catchment, was developed to study and understand catchment-scale trade-offs of rainwater harvesting (RWH). The model incorporates an effective representation of RWH function and impact, and works on a daily time step. Catchment spatial variability is captured through sub-basins. Within each sub-basin hydrological response units (HRUs) describe the different land use/soil combinations associated with the case study catchment, including irrigated agriculture. Sustainability indices, based on irrigated agri- culture water demand, were used to compare conceptual management scenarios. The results show that as RWH area increases, it reaches a limiting capacity from where additional RWH structures do not increase the benefit to groundwater stores, but reduces stream flow. If the irrigation area is increased at the optimal level of RWH, where the sustainability indices were greatest, the resilience of the sys- tem actually decreased. Nevertheless RWH in a system increased the overall sustainability of the water

knowledge.evidence: Rainwater harvesting (RWH) is a small-scale catchment devel- opment tool with a long tradition in many countries, including India (Agarwal and Narain, 1997). In many parts of India RWH captures and stores the intensive monsoonal runoff to recharge groundwater. Where RWH is present, it increases the capacity of small-holder farmers to irrigate with groundwater, so there is a greater need to understand how this catchment development tool impacts larger scale catchment water balances. The resulting shifts in the water balance could impact the resilience of agricultural livelihoods, which means communities could be more vulnerable to shocks such as drought (Mudrakartha, 2007). An individual RWH structure may not have a large effect on stream flow or aquifer storage, but the cumulative effect of many RWH structures within a large catchment would be more significant. For example the con- struction of farm dams in some catchments of the Murray Darling Basin in Australia caused statistically significant reductions in the quantity of potential stream flow response (Schreider et al., 2002).

Hydrological response units Within each sub-basin hydrological response units (HRU) are defined, which represent a land use with unique management fac- tors and soil type and have no spatial interpretation (Arnold and Fohrer, 2005). The water balance is calculated for each HRU in each sub-basin. The partitioning of rainfall into runoff uses the USDA-SCS Curve Number method (USDA-SCS, 1985). All runoff is first routed into the RWH reservoirs, where a maximum depth for RWH is defined. Any water that overflows from the RWH reser- voir is moved into the stream, which is then routed into the next sub-basin, subject to transmission losses. The dominant land uses in the Arvari River catchment were incorporated into the conceptual model. Current land use in the Arvari River catchment closely reflects elevation and soil distribu- tion. In the hills, with higher elevations and shallow rocky soils, land is usually used for grazing with thinly covered forest areas or open land known as commons. In the plains along the river, where the soils are deeper and richer in clay content, land use is predominantly agriculture, including irrigated agriculture. All runoff is first routed into the RWH reservoirs, where a maximum depth for RWH is defined. knowledge.evidence: 3.1.6. Interception and runoff The USDA-SCS Curve Number (CN) was used to estimate runoff from each land use. The CN method predicts runoff from rain- fall, using a curve number, which represents potential maximum soil retention and reflects land use, antecedent moisture condi- tion and soils (Ponce and Hawkins, 1996). On larger temporal scales, initial losses increase due to transmission and evaporation losses (Simanton et al., 1996). However on a daily time step ini- tial abstraction (Ia) is small. Therefore Ia was changed from 0.3 to 0.05 (Woodward et al., 2003). Antecedent moisture conditions 2 and hydrologic soil group B (medium textured soils) were used to find the CN for each land use. The CN for each agriculture HRU and commons HRU was defined from the SCS tables (USDA-SCS, 1985), which are similar to a study for south-eastern Rajasthan, where weighted CN values ranged from 80 to 83 (Gupta et al., 1997). However the CN is a calibration parameter in the model and might increase or decrease for real catchments. The agriculture land uses have two curve numbers, a CN of 77 during the time when land is fallow and a lower CN of 72 when cropped. The commons land use CN was set to 79.

To better under- stand the response of the model to the input parameters, a limited sensitivity analysis was performed with the parameters considered to have the highest impact on the output of the model (Lenhart et al., 2002). The parameters CN, Ia, LAI, FC, percolation coefficient, irriga- tion trigger, AWcr, and WP, were considered to have the highest impact. Additionally, to understand how the spatial and temporal variability of rainfall might affect the output, rainfall was included in the sensitivity analysis. The sums of Johad recharge and Bandh recharge, shallow aquifer water levels, runoff, ET and stream flow were used as output variables. For each output a Relative Sensitivity Index was calculated (Lenhart et al., 2002; Ouessar et al., 2008).

This adjustment was aimed to improve the representation of the main processes related to RWH in a semi-arid catchment, in this case the Arvari River catchment. As such, the adjustment brings the model in the realm of possible real catchments rather than purely theoretical. It was observed that local farmers increase the area of irri- gated agriculture based on the groundwater availability, which they judge from the water levels in their dug wells. The actual groundwater use is a complex function, which relates to how the farmers adjust the irrigation area to groundwater availability. knowledge.evidence: To meet crop water demands in the Arvari River, the farmers rely on a combination of groundwater and rainfall in Kharif and groundwater in Rabi. Kharif, the summer or monsoon crop, which is mostly maize, is planted after the first rains in July and har- vested in October. Rabi, the winter crop, mainly wheat, is planted in November and harvested around March. The water resource sys- tem was therefore based on the availability of water in the sowing months of the Kharif (July) and Rabi (November) crops. The daily available water in the system is defined as the groundwater stor- age combined with any rainfall. Because the initial available water at the start of each season strongly determines water availability for the rest of the season and the amount of irrigated area planted, any impact of RWH is best based on the first month of each sea- son (July and November). The water available was compared with a defined threshold to calculate daily values of the sustainability indices. For maximum production, a medium maturity maize crop, grown in Kharif season, requires between 500 and 800 mm of water depending on the climate. The water required to irrigate maize to maturity using the FAO crop factors, is 511.8 mm for 125 growing

This means that variations in rainfall across sub-basins would strongly impact the output distribution, which was also seen in the field where recharge from RWH was clearly affected by rainfall (Glendenning and Vervoort, 2010). The parameters with the high- est sensitivity are CN and Ia, which for all output had medium to very high sensitivity, because CN and Ia determine the partitioning of rainfall into runoff. The most sensitive output is the groundwa- ter level, which was sensitive to each parameter change. Given that this study is focussed on a conceptual comparison, the sensitivity of the model to the groundwater levels is quite important, as this is the key state variable that RWH would influence. However, the high sensitivity would be a problem for making more location specific statements given the high parameter uncertainty. knowledge.evidence: bility. At low irrigation area (5%), vulnerability is negligible, but increases with each step in irrigation area. At 15% irrigation, in both crop seasons, as RWH increases from 0.5% RWH to 1% area, vulnerability increases. However from 1.5 to 3% RWH area, the vul- nerability stabilises (Fig. 6). At 10% irrigation in the Kharif season a similar response was seen in the reliability analysis of the Rabi season (Fig. 4), which is the result of the increase in irrigation area. Compared to the first analysis with irrigation and no RWH (Fig. 3), the addition of RWH in the system increases reliability, resilience and decreases the vulnerability of the water resource system for irrigated agriculture. Within an individual irrigation sce- nario, as RWH area doubles from 1.5 to 3%, the benefit to the system is not large and in some cases the sustainability indices actually decrease. This suggests that there is a limit in the area of RWH that gives a maximum recharge benefit and beyond which the benefit is marginal. In addition, the fact that farmers respond to water levels and increase their irrigation area means that some levels of RWH area are less sustainable depending on management practices.

As such the model has 23 parameters (Table 3). Compared to a low parameter model such as IHACRES (Evans and Jakeman, 1998) it is complex. knowledge.evidence: RWH. Kumar et al. (2006) argue that RWH has an extremely limited potential to provide reliable water supply, because of high rain- fall variability and high PotET. In contrast, the conceptual analysis here shows that while the sustainability indices decrease when drought occurs, the modelled system functions better with RWH than without. Another important aspect of RWH impacts are the hydrologi- cal changes in a catchment, which were examined by comparing stream flow changes under different scenarios. When RWH is introduced, stream flow strongly decreases. Capturing local runoff upstream in RWH storages addresses problems of frequent drought and widespread poverty in upper catchments. However the ‘blue’ water investments, like irrigation canals, are generally located downstream (for example Sainthal Sagar Dam in the Arvari River catchment) and depend on large volumes of runoff (Sakthivadivel, 2008). As RWH leads to an increase in ‘green’ water used for irrigated agriculture upstream, this will affect ‘blue’ water avail- ability for downstream users, including irrigators and ecosystems, because flows decrease. However RWH could also have positive environmental impacts as a result of reduced land degradation.

Finally longer residence times increases possi- ble feedbacks between water and vegetation and could lead to improved environmental condition. This would require further field analysis. source.title: Balancing watershed and local scale impacts of rain water harvesting in India—A review

knowledge.evidence: production in India has become increasingly reliant on groundwater and this has resulted in depletion of groundwater resources. Rainwater harvesting (RWH) for groundwater recharge is seen as one of the solutions to solve the groundwater problem. This is reflected in an increase in watershed development programs, in which RWH is an important structural component. Understanding the net effect of these development programs is crucial to ensure that net effect on groundwater is positive both locally and within a watershed. Hence, this review focuses on the hydrological impacts of RWH for recharge at the local (individual structure) and watershed scale in rural areas. Surprisingly little field evidence of the stated positive impacts at the local scale is available, and there are several potential negative impacts at the watershed scale. The watershed scale is underrepresented in the field studies and is mainly approached through modelling. Modelling is seen as a possible tool to extend limited field data and scenario studies can be used to examine potential impacts. However, many past modelling studies examining RWH have either had limited focus or have been based on insufficient data. Development

In practice, the impact of RWH on the hydrological balance of a watershed is that water is stored and delayed with a transfer of surface runoff into groundwater, evaporation and transpira- tion. This can also be understood as the transfer of ‘blue’ water (rivers and aquifers) to ‘green’ water (soil water and plant water use). As more water is ‘captured’ through irrigated land use, blue water is converted into green water (Falkenmark, 2003). The poten- tial increase in available groundwater may encourage increased groundwater abstraction for crop irrigation or other uses resulting in socio-economic impacts, while the impact on the water bal- ance may be zero or negative. Hence, in general, RWH will change the water balance within a watershed. One reason for the lack of studies on the impact of RWH is because measuring the average recharge of many RWH structures across a watershed can be difficult, expensive and time consum- ing due to high spatial and temporal variability in landscape and climatic conditions. As Section 3.2 will show, many field studies of RWH impact are based on calculating recharge using the water balance. However, recharge is one of the most difficult components of the water bal- ance to measure, because it needs to be measured below the visible surface and is highly variable. (1998) quantified the effects of RWH in 16 observa- tion wells in Maharashtra state, by modelling groundwater coupled with a water balance model, and concluded that there was an over- all increase in groundwater recharge from RWH of 16%, which is an increase of 2% of the local annual rainfall. Using the HYLUC (Hydrological Land Use Change) model in Andhra Pradesh, rainwa- ter harvesting was suggested to cause the closure of a basin (Calder et al., 2008), which means no more water would flow further down- stream. However, increased siltation in the RWH structures caused downstream flows to increase again. Continued and new research into the areas identified in this review would greatly assist further policy development. We have highlighted a major lack of quantifiable hydrological studies at the watershed scale and also a lack of local scale data. While models are pow- erful and will continue to play a role in management of RWH, further model development and integration with new data sources is needed. There is very little understanding of the impact of sil- tation on the RWH structure hydrology and how siltation may be managed. Aspects of water quality and the interplay between RWH for recharge and groundwater salinity are also lacking from the reviewed research. knowledge.evidence: In the dryland regions, it is well known that poor rainfall distribution leads to dry periods that often decrease yield poten- tial (HarvestChoice, 2010). While there are many opportunities for management to increase water use efficiency (WUE) via a range of agronomic management practices in broadacre systems (Kirkegaard et al., 2014a) including rotations (Whitbread et al., 2015), tillage systems and residue management (Kirkegaard et al., 2014b; Thierfelder and Wall, 2009), in the Indian context small farm size limits the impacts of such interventions. Therefore the storage and later reuse of rainfall via irrigation represent a widely promoted intensification strategy in India (Keller et al., 2000; Reddy et al., 2012; Malik et al., 2013). In this paper, we present and discuss the impact of public programmes which have implemented farm level rainwater harvesting schemes across 5 states.
knowledge.finding: Findings relate to evapotranspiration, rainfall, rainwater harvesting, water use efficiency.

To ensure safe to drink water quality from the tanka, the structure needed proper concrete roof with covered opening (with locking system) as well as cleaning of catchment. Most of the farmers took such measure for ensuring water quality. With 30–40,000 L RWHS, the farmers could plant 50–60 arid fruit plants, for example Zyziphus moritiana and Cordia myxa recommended for these areas (Pareek, 1999; Pareek and Awasthi, 2008). That gave an additional annual net return of US $ 195 from the third year onwards. But the adoption of small Tanka with horticulture plants was low mainly due to lack of awareness and knowledge, lack of capital, long payback period (>5 years) and poor targeting of farm- ers (Kumar and Roy, 2013). The capital requirement for a ‘Tanka’ of 60–70,000 L capacity, the size required to support an economically viable 1 ha orchard (Kumar and Roy, 2013), are much higher.

knowledge.evidence: analysis indicates that the integration of farm pond in the dryland farming systems has great potential to increase farm productivity and income in these regions. However, its adoption and net benefits varied significantly among different house- holds/districts/states. In the multiple linear regression analysis, the coefficients for landholding size and household assets were signif- icant indicating that the benefits of RWHS significantly increased with an increase in the size of landholding and household assets (Table 8). This result is supported by the observation that farmers with less than 2.0 ha landholdings in dry areas were not willing to adopt farm ponds. The landholding size of our sample house- holds was also more than 2 ha in all the districts except Chittoor and Bangalore rural. The small farmers for whom agriculture is not the major source of income, during FGD’s stated that they do not want to lose land for the RWHS and adoption of RWHS affects their wage earning activities adversely as they need to allocate labour and other resources for construction and management of farm ponds. This was also supported by (AICRPDA, 1991-2011).

However, the two funnel graphs look fairly like funnels, which may indicate a publication selection bias or not. In addition, the funnel asymmetry test can be conducted (Tables 7 and 8). knowledge.evidence: Water is a limiting natural resource for agricultural production. While it is well accepted that crop types differ in their water use efficiency (WUE), there is no consensus on the main factors affecting WUE of main field crops, which was the motivation of the current study. The effects of rainfall pattern, soil type and climatic regime on crop WUE were evaluated using data from 514 experiments around the world published in ISI journal papers. The results confirmed that crop type had a significant effect (p < 0.05) on WUE with cereals producing on average 2.37 kg of dry grain per cubic meter (m−3) of water followed by oilseeds (0.69 kg m−3), fibre crops (0.45 kg m−3) and legumes (0.42 kg m−3). Amongst cereals, maize (3.78 kg m−3) and sorghum (2.52 kg m−3) were more water-use efficient than wheat (1.02 kg m−3), barley (1.21 kg m−3) and millet (0.47 kg m−3). Overall, maize was the most water use efficient crop under well-watered conditions (9.90 kg m−3), but sorghum was the most efficient under dry conditions (5.99 kg m−3). WUE of crops increased from desert to tropical through sub-tropical climate. Globally, agriculture accounts for 80–90 % of all freshwater used by humans, and most of that water is used for crop production (Morison et al., 2008). While irrigation de- velopment has increased crop productivity in arid and semi-arid areas for decades, water scarcity and escalating costs of setting and managing the infrastructure hamper further expansion of irrigation in developing countries. Rising demand for water by other sectors such as domestic, mining, industries, the environment and, recently, severe pressures from climate uncertainties, exacerbates water shortages for further ir- rigation development. knowledge.evidence: total irrigation water transpired to water diverted from the source (Israelsen, 1932), while crop scientists define it as the ratio of total biomass or grain yield to water supplied (Sharma et al., 2015). The present paper adopted WUE as the ratio of grain yield achieved to the amount of water made available to the crop (i.e. stored in the soil plus rainfall and irrigation water). It is expressed as grain yield per unit of land area (Y, kg m−2) divided by the amount of water consumed by the crop per unit land area (ET, m3 m−2), usually reported as mm of water needed to produce that yield (Blum, 2005). The need for crops to be drought tolerant and have higher WUE has been the focus of breeding efforts for many years (Sivamani et al., 2000; Tilman et al., 2002; Condon et al., 2004; Blum, 2005; Ruggiero et al., 2017) to alleviate water scarcity and food insecurity. Improved soil fertility and crop management practices have also been developed to enhance better yields with less water (Evans and Sadler, 2008; Busari and Salako, 2013; Busari et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018). However, water scarcity remains an issue and there is still need for better un- derstanding of the underlying controls of crop WUE.

Impact of crop type on WUE The mean WUE was 1.74 ± 0.11 kg m−3 with values ranging from 0.03 kg m−3 for wheat in China to 14.8 kg m−3 for maize in Ethiopia (Meskelu et al., 2014) (Table 4). Summer crops had higher WUE (average of 3.23 kg m−3) than winter crops (1.03 kg m−3), a 3.13 times difference, significant at P < 0.05 (Fig. 2). Cereals had the highest WUE (2.37 kg m−3) amongst the cultivated crop types studied (Fig. 3). WUE decreased from cereals to oilseed crops (0.69 kg m−3), fibre crops (0.45 kg m−3) and to legumes (0.45 kg m−3), all the differences were significant at P < 0.05. Amongst cereals, maize (mean of 3.78 kg m−3) had 1.5 fold greater WUE than sorghum (2.52 kg m−3) (Fig. 4). The WUE decreased to barley (1.21 kg m−3), wheat (1.02 kg m−3) and to pearl millet (0.47 kg m−3). Linseed (0.21 kg m−3) and mustard (0.17 kg m−3) had the lowest WUE in the data set (Fig. 4).

The increase in WUE was of 81 %, from desert to subtropical and by 134 % from subtropical to tropical. In deserts (Fig. 6A), sorghum had the highest WUE (5.99 kg m−3) and was fol- lowed by maize (1.20 kg m−3), sunflower (0.93 kg m−3) and pea (0.62 kg m−3). Under subtropical conditions (Fig. 6B), maize had the highest WUE (2.32 kg m−3) and was followed by sorghum (1.49 kg m−3). Surprisingly, WUE of barley and wheat did not significantly differ, as this of sunflower, millet, cotton and pea (Fig. 6B). Under the tropical climate, maize had significantly higher WUE (9.90 kg m−3) which was 9.5 times higher than for sorghum (1.04 kg m−3) whilst WUE of millet, safflower, linseed and mustard were all below 0.3 kg m−3 (Fig. 6C). Under temperate climate (Fig. 6 D), maize had the highest WUE (1.17 kg m−3), but was not significantly different from wheat (0.97 kg m−3), sorghum (0.4 kg m−3) and cotton (0.24 kg m−3), probably owing to low number of data points. The increase of WUE with precipitation was confirmed by correlation coefficient (r) of 0.52

knowledge.evidence: 4.2.2. Soil texture The present study confirms the impact of soil texture on WUE (Mojid et al., 2012). Soil clay content appeared to have a strong ne- gative impact on crop WUE (r=−0.78, p < 0.01) (Table 5) with high clay soil contents tending to depress crop yields. This trend was, how- ever, invalidated for maize most likely because maize does well in most soil types (Bennetzen and Hake, 2008). High clay contents are most of the time associated with waterlogging conditions and low soil water holding capacity, both detrimental to crop yield (Greenway et al., 2006; Morales-Olmedo et al., 2015). Another interesting result was the trend for WUE to be highest under both silt-loam and loam textures (Fig. 8A, C), which are known to be associated with fertile soils (Russel, 2002).

knowledge.evidence: The study investigated the impacts of soil and environmental con- ditions on water use efficiency (WUE) of main field crops. The first main conclusion using data from 514 sites across the globe was that crops differed significantly in their abilities to efficiently use water for grain yield, with C4 plants such as maize exhibiting significantly higher WUE than C3 types (e.g. wheat). The second conclusion was climate had significant impact on water use efficiency with a tendency for warm and wet climates to yield higher crop WUE than cooler en- vironments. The third conclusion was that soil texture significantly impacted crop WUE with lowest values occurring in clayey soils and highest values under loamy conditions. However, maize performed very well in all soil textures. There is still a certain level of unexplained variability in crop WUE that could potentially be attributed to factors not considered in the present study, which are seldom reported in lit- erature on WUE such as seasonal variations of climate, land manage- ment and agronomic practices such as fertilization application, tillage and crop residue mulching. knowledge.evidence: Relevant peer-reviewed studies from 1997 to 2020 were collected. The search engines used in this article included Google Scholar (https:// xueshu.soogle.top/), Elsevier (Science Direct) (https://www.scienc edirect.com/search) and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (htt ps://www.cnki.net/) using the key words: “partial root drying” OR “deficit irrigation” OR “partial root-zone” OR “irrigation strategies/re­ gimes” OR “water-saving irrigation” AND “water use efficiency” AND “yield”. In total, there were 90 publications, including 305 pairs of ob­ servations of yield and WUE that satisfied our criteria for the meta- analysis. The list of the 90 publications from which the data were extracted are listed in Appendix A. These publications were screened using the following criteria. knowledge.evidence: In this meta-analysis, we found that the response of crop yields and WUE to APRI and DI varied significantly in response to irrigation management practices relative to FULL, including irrigation strategy, deficit stage and proportion (Figs. 4–6). Regardless of DI or APRI (compared with FULL) or APRI compared with DI, changes of yield of drip irrigation showed a larger decrease compared to furrow irrigation (Figs. 4a–6a). This may be because the reduced irrigation water used in furrow irrigation was able to improve the oxygen content in soils and reduced nutrient loss caused by anaerobic respiration, while drip irri­ gation has been verified as a means of regular and even water supply (Cetin and Bilgel, 2002; Yu et al., 2020). As for drip irrigation, the water condition of crops under drip irrigation was probably inherently better than that of furrow irrigation, so the reduced water supply under drip irrigation resulted in a reduction in yield (Camp, 1998). However, WUE of pairwise comparisons of irrigation methods were all significantly increased compared to the control treatment (Figs. 4b–6b). This can be largely attributed to the reduced evapotranspiration (Sezen and Yazar, 2006).

There was no significant difference in yield between APRI and DI, but WUE under APRI was higher. knowledge.evidence: The agricultural activities contribute to the largest share of water consumption in the arid and semi-arid basins. In this study, we demonstrate the application of Water Accounting Plus (WA+) for estimation of the green water consumption (ETGreen) and blue water consumption (ETBlue) for assessing the water productivity (WP) and land productivity (LP) to identify the bright-spots and hot-spots at the district administrative unit level for effectively managing the scarce water resources and sustaining food security in a highly non-resilient semi-arid basin of India. The WA+ framework uses satellite remote sensing datasets from different sources for this purpose and we used the data from 2003 to 2020. The long-term average of ETGreen and ETBlue in the Mahi basin is found to be 15.8 km3/year and 12.32 km3/year, respectively. The blue water index (BWI) and green water index (GWI) in the basin vary from 0.282 to 0.598 and 0.40–0.72. knowledge.evidence: Increasing water productivity (WP) and land productivities (LP) for sustaining food security and freshwater availability is a significant challenge to the current and future generations (Safi et al., 2022). The water availability for agricultural production will decrease due to increased competition from industrial and domestic sectors (Zwart and Bastiaanssen, 2007) and this will eventually put excess pressure on the farmers. This is the reason that there is a growing emphasis on increasing WP in agriculture (Kang et al., 2017; Marston et al., 2020; Molden, 2007; Bastiaanssen et al., 2003). WP is represented as the ratio of the crop yield to the green and blue water consumption (i.e., ETgreen and ETBlue), where ETGreen and ETBlue represent the actual evapo­ transpiration (ET) due to green water and blue water, respectively

Recently, the WA+ framework has emerged as a key tool for understanding the water-food nexus and identifying the gaps and inefficiencies in water uses. WA+ framework is based on the fundamental concept of water ‘depletions’ as that of IWMI-WA rather than ‘withdrawals’ and segregates these depletions into ETgreen and ETBlue using the popular Budyko (1974) hypothesis. The coupling between the landuse and land cover with the water consumption patterns is an essential information, particularly, for the arid regions evaluation of water management strategies and policy making (Peiser and Bastiaanssen, 2015). The Budyko curve represents the empirical relationship between the ET, PET & P (Sposito, 2017) by representing the ratio of ET and P as Evaporative Index (EI) and PET and P as Dryness Index (DI). The Budyko curve is highly altered (i.e., the points (EI and DI)) due to extensive human interventions, particularly, due to irrigation, where the P is not the only source to meet consumptive demands (Chen et al., 2020; Si­ mons et al., 2020). Generally, ET/P should not exceed unity until and unless additional water is added to the basin. The Water balance approach and Energy balance approaches are incorporated into the Budyko hypothesis. A separate water balance calculation is done for each of the green and blue pixels, which identifies the rainfed and irrigated areas. Water-limited catchments (ϕ > 1) and energy-limited catchments (ϕ < 1) are sepa­ rated by this notion (Singh et al., 2022) (Fig. 7). knowledge.evidence: We know that green water is the sole water source for rainfed agri­ culture and an important part of the water source for irrigated croplands (Li et al., 2022). Agriculture is the only sector where green and blue water both contribute mutually (Liu et al., 2022) and that crop irrigation consumes the largest proportion of blue water (Mekonnen and Hoekstra, 2012). (Mao et al., 2020) state that even though green water is the dominant water resource, blue water is also critical which is back into the soil through physical and human-induced processes to meet the water demand of the ecosystem. In this study, ETBlue and ETGreen are quantified using the Budyko hypothesis. The results show that the long-term average annual ETGreen in the basin is 15.8 km3 /year which is 1.28 times higher than the ETBlue (12.32 km3/year). The district-wise estimates of the long-term monthly average of ETGreen and ETBlue are shown in Fig. 11 and the spatial variability is shown in Fig. 12 (a-b). In general, the results show that the districts falling in the Gujarat state have more ETBlue followed by the districts in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh. We also calculated the blue water index (BWI = ETBlue/(ET­ Blue+ETGreen)) and green water index (GWI = ETGreen/(ET­ Blue+ETGreen)) , and the results are given in Table 3. An index value of 1 shows that the crop yield is from irrigation only, whereas an index of 0 indicates that precipitation is sufficient to achieve maximum crop yields (Johansson et al., 2016). WA+ estimates of WP and LP are highly dependent on the irrigated and rainfed crop map of the basin this necessitates for field surveys of cropping patterns for enhanced performance. Finally, the WA+ based LULC map (WALU) needs to be customized for local conditions (say region-specific) as the many classes (out of 80 classes) are not applicable to all the regions of the world. We took the cereals as the major crop class in the basin as without segregating them into wheat and paddy due to the absence of a detailed and accurate crop map area of the Mahi basin. This aspect also needs a major refinement to estimate crop-wise LP and WP in the basin. (Salvadore et al., 2020) also emphasized and accurate and detailed crop map of the basin to estimate the crop wise yield productivity. Heavy dependence of the WA+ technique on the satellite datasets limits this technique’s applicability to future assessments incorporating climate change scenarios. The WA+ technique does not have the snow glacier component, and this limits its applicability to the glacier basins.

knowledge.evidence: In arid and semi-arid regions, agricultural activities have the largest proportion of the water consumption, and therefore this study was formulated to estimate the green and blue water consumption (ETBlue and ETGreen) and assess the spatial and temporal variability of the WP and LP to identify the bright-spots and hot-spots at the district admin­ istrative unit level for effectively managing the scarce water resources and sustaining food security in highly non-resilient basin of India. The findings will ultimately help formulate the “actionable management plans” to the stakeholders and policymakers of the Mahi basin. How­ ever, to address the limitations of the WA+ technique as discussed above, this technique should be coupled with a hydrological model say Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) and Spatial Processes in Hy­ drology (SPHY) model to address the current and future status of the water availability, demand, and supply scenarios. This ensemble modelling framework (WA+ coupled with the SWAT and SPHY) may also include the socio-economic aspects in the devising of actionable water management plans.

knowledge.evidence: As the WP (both irrigated and rainfed) of the districts of Gujarat such as Anand, Vadodara, Kheda, and Bharuch is lower than that of the dis­ tricts of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan in the Mahi basin and hence advanced irrigation techniques coupled with the crop diversification (adopting the technological and agronomical interventions of the bright spot districts such as Ratlam and Neemach) to increase the WP without effecting the LP of these hot-spot districts. The higher values of BWI are an indication of the more dependency on irrigation for agricultural production and hence efforts should be made to incentivize the farmers for crop diversification and shifting from more water intensive crops to less water-intensive crops. These findings can be taken as ‘baseline’ for developing ‘actionable agricultural water management plans’ by the stakeholders and policymakers of the basin states.

knowledge.evidence: Life on earth is linked to water resources. Recently, alarm bells have been ringing in global organizations to raise awareness of the importance of rational use of water resources, which are becoming an increasingly scarce commodity. The majority of the world’s freshwater is used for agricultural irrigation, hence there is a need to adopt an intelligent irrigation strategy that will lead to sustainable agricultural management. To reap the full benefits, irrigation strategy must be accompanied by a good understanding of field characteristics. Several studies have benefited from the improvement of new technologies for irrigation scheduling, but taking only soil water properties as a basis for research, and to our knowledge there is no systematic literature review study to date that aims at irrigation scheduling taking into consideration the characteristics of the crop field for intelligent and efficient agricultural management. This literature review article aims to explore the new Internet of Things and Artificial Intelligence technologies used on the one hand for monitoring and predicting the coefficients that control the crop evapotranspiration process responsible for crop water losses, namely the reference crop

Following a systematic literature review meth­ odology led us to a refined selection of 55 journal articles for further analysis. We have identified that the profitability of a crop field is closely linked to the right strategies adopted in a specific crop plot, and these strategies can only be defined after a good understanding of the field’s characteristics. Excessive use of water resources, espe­ cially in the agricultural sector, which is responsible for consuming most of the world’s freshwater, is making these resources less and less available. ETo is a complex and non-linear parameter that is therefore difficult to measure and is influenced by several meteorological factors, which, combined together, affect the soil evap­ oration process. ETo is generally evaluated by means of empirical and semi-empirical equations in which temperature, wind speed and humidity are forming some of the key climatological data that provide the energy required for evaporation and remove water vapour from the evaporating surface (Anderson and French, 2019). According to these results, the irrigation scheduling is not only dependent on climatic changes due to weather conditions, but also on the biophysical responses of crops summarized in the crop coefficient Kc, which in turn is affected by several factors that are the physical, chemical, biological and hydrological characteristics of the soil. RQ2: What factors have a significant influence on the crop coefficient Kc as mentionned in FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper? The value of the Kc coefficient varies considerably according to a number of factors including crop-specific factors such as crop type, season and growth stage, etc., soil-related factors such as the physical, chemical and biological properties of the soil, and agricultural practices. knowledge.evidence: Micro-irrigation, known for enhancing water use efficiency and crop yields, is subject to the phenomenon of the Jevons paradox or rebound effect. Farmers adopting the technology also tend to adopt economic mechanisms – extensive (increasing operated area) and intensive (changing crop patterns). We studied the question of the rebound effect using primary data from four states of India – Maharashtra, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh. Recall data from 404 sample farmers were collected on crop area, land use, and water use in a pre- and post-micro-irrigation adoption scenario. The data analysis suggests that most farmers agreed they increased their cropped area after micro-irrigation. The recall data of area change under various crops showed that more than 85 % of farmers increased their area post the adoption of micro-irrigation. Along with the in- crease in total operated area, farmers brought an additional 267 ha (17 %) under irrigated agriculture, out of which about 87 ha were converted from rainfed to irrigated areas under various crops. Farmers converted a substantial area from cereals to high-value horticulture crops. knowledge.evidence: 2 Micro-irrigation technology has shown to help farmers produce more from less inputs - water, fertilisers, labour, and energy, and thus enhance their incomes (Gandhi et al., 2021; Mattoussi et al., 2023; Nar- ayanamoorthy, 2005; Scheierling et al., 2006a; Viswanathan et al., 2016). knowledge.evidence: Water use efficiency can be enhanced through technologies such as micro-irrigation, mulching, cover crop. These efficiencies can be cat- egorised as - technical, cost, and productivity (G´omez and P´erez-Blanco, 2014). Technical efficiency measures the effect of input use on output; cost efficiency assesses how a technology can save costs for a given output level; and productivity measures output obtained per unit of water. Although all are desirable, enhanced water productivity can lead to increased water consumption as farmers aim to boost profits through expanded cropping areas and altered patterns (G´omez and P´erez-Blanco, 2014; Fishman et al., 2023; Wheeler et al., 2020). The phenomenon - the rebound effect or Jevons paradox, is more pronounced among farmers with larger water rights, as they exercise their rights to over extract groundwater, leading to spatial externalities and water inequity that affect other farmers in the same basin (H. Li and Zhao, 2018). The paradox manifests through expanded cultivation areas, shifts to water-intensive crops, and increased water usage behaviours among farmers after the adoption of micro irrigation. A comprehensive un- derstanding of these mechanisms is essential for effective policy

Studies in regions such as New Mexico’s Rio Grande Project (Brinegar and Ward, 2009) and the Upper Rio Grande basin (Dagnino and Ward, 2012) indicate that while subsidies for water-saving technologies enhance water use efficiency, they also increase crop water consumption through evapotranspiration. Higher crop growth and yields exacerbate water losses due to increased biological water demand, as evidenced in Cal- ifornia’s Westlands water district (Burt et al., 2001). Lopez-Gunn et al. (2012) observed similar trends in Spain, where efficiency gains from MI did not translate into actual water conservation due to increased evapotranspiration and overall water consumption in cropping systems. In another study in the Upper Rio Grande Basin, water efficiency im- provements correlated positively with crop yield and subsequent addi- tional evapotranspiration due to MI (Ward and Pulido-Velazquez, 2008). The adoption of new agricultural technology by farmers is generally driven by economic incentives rather than solely by water conservation

Economic gains, such as reduced opera- tional costs in irrigation and increased yields, steer farmers toward profit-maximising behaviours upon implementing micro-irrigation (MI) technology (Song et al., 2018). The behavioural shift includes altering cropping patterns, changing crop densities, expanding cultivation areas, and switching to more water-intensive crop varieties, reflecting farmers’ prioritisation of economic outcomes over water conservation, termed the economic mechanism (Wheeler et al., 2020; Fishman et al., 2023; Song et al., 2018). The study by Patil et al. (2015) found that the adoption of micro-irrigation resulted in an increase in both gross-irrigated area and farmer income without a significant surge in groundwater use. Fishman et al. (2023) examined the impact of drip irrigation subsidies in Andhra Pradesh through a randomized control trial. Over three years, it found that farmers switched to more profitable horticulture crops, leading to increased profitability. The farmers sold the saved water to neighbouring farmers, resulting in no significant decline in groundwater extraction. However, these previous studies were limited in their geographical scope and context, and they did not offer comprehensive understanding of the paradox’s dynamics. This limitation presented for us an opportunity to further explore the paradox and deepen our understanding. The economic and hydrological mech- anisms post MI technology adoption can have unintended implications for government water conservation efforts. knowledge.evidence: Table 3 presents key descriptive statistics from the data. On average, farmers operate 3.17 ha of land, with the average technology intensi- ty—percentage area under the technology compared to total operated land—standing at 68 %. The cropping intensity averaged 1.41 before micro-irrigation and increased to 1.49 after adoption, indicating a rise in the gross area under crops. The Herfindahl index, a measure of crop concentration or diversification on the farm, averaged 0.581 before adoption and 0.559 post-adoption. A higher Herfindahl index signifies greater concentration (less diversification), suggesting an increase in crop diversification following MI adoption, as discussed in the analysis section. Other statistics include the average distance of 15 km to the nearest market from the farm, and an average household size of about six members. Farmers have, on average, about nine years of formal education, with an average age of 47 years.
