knowledge.evidence: water harvesting system that uses a portion of the land as catchment to harvest runoff and divert it to adjacent crop area can prove beneficial. Numerous catchment construction materials have been used for increasing the runoff. Compacted earth catchment is the cheapest one but its runoff yields are poor. On the other hand, catchments treated with paraffin wax, silicon, butyl rubber, p,lastic and sheet metal can produce nearly 100 per cent runoff (Cooley et al. 1975), but are very expensive. In arid situation, Singh (1988a) treated the catchment with pond sediment and recorded that from 0.5 catchment to crop area ratio, each ha of crop area received 140 to 636 mm of rainwater, while the rainfall received was 117 to 528 mm in different years. In this case average runoff efficiency was 66 per cent. As a result, 3717 kg of pearl millet grain ha-! was obtained with only 69 per cent of normal rainfall (Singh 1988b). Substantial reductions in yield due to plant water stress at critical growth stages may occur even though the total amount of water delivered during the cropping season may be adequate (Jensen et al. 1990). Howell & Hiler (1975) ob- served that linear regression with ET eXplained only 41 per cent variability in sorghum yield. Booting to bloom stage was the most sensitive to water stress. Similarly, the greatest adverse effect of water stress on yield and WUE of wheat was observed during jointing and flowering stage (Singh et al. 1986), whereas, Tripathi et al. (1989) found the crown root initiation stage to be the most critical stage in wheat. Plants exhibiting crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM) open their stomates at night and fix C02 in malic acid, which is then assimilated during the day by C3 pathway while stomates remain closed. The closed stomates during the day time reduce transpiration to almost negligible level. knowledge.evidence: Water retained in soil is lost through ·the combined process of evaporation from soil and transpiration from plants. Reducing this loss would be important for both decreasing crop water requirement and, under certain environ- --mental conditions, for alleviation of water stress. One of the common practices to reduce evapora- tion from soil is the use of mulches. Maintaining a crop residue mulch on soil surface may also increase soil water content by reducing runoff and increasing infilt~ation rate due to reduced soil dispersion an.d surface sealing. Mulches reduce evaporation by reflecting part of the in- coming solar radiation that otherwise would be absorbed as heat; by acting as a thermal insulator and thus restricting the flow of heat from at- mosphere to soil; and by increasing the thickness of still air layer above the soil surface that increases the resistance to vapour transfer from soil surface to atmosphere. 24 22 20

knowledge.evidence: Since residue mulches reduce evaporation from the wet soil surfaces, these are most effective during the rainy season when evaporation rate is high from bare soil surface. Slowing the evapora- tion rate in these conditions favours deeper soil moisture penetration. At the end of rainy season (or after irrigation) when drying starts the rate of water loss from a residue covered soil is higher (Fig. 3) because the surface soil remains wet for much longer period; thus over a longer period, cumulative water loss may be almost equal in mulched and bare soils.

knowledge.evidence: objective to develop efficient and high yielding varieties of crops: An enormous effort has been expended on this objective. Impressive results have been achieved in a few crops only. For major crops high yielding varieties are yet to come which should have high response to applied fertilizers and should efficiently use the other inputs including water. The quantum jump with respect to all these is yet to come. The varieties should also be pest and disease resistant which indirectly influence the WUE. The use of trickle or drip irrigation though saves considerable quan- tities of irrigation water and gives higher WOE under limited water supply conditions also has some limitations of use. Some important possible disadvantages of trickle irrigation compared to other irrigation methods include (1) emitter clogg- ing, (2) rodent and other animal damage, (3) salt accumulation near the plants, (4) inadequate soil water movement and plant root development, and (5) econom~cal and technical limitations (Bucks et al. 1982).

source.title: Sustainable Groundwater Management in India Needs a Water‐Energy‐Food Nexus Approach

knowledge.evidence: Groundwater depletion in India is a result of water, energy, and food pol- icies that have given rise to a nexus where growth in agriculture has been supported by unsustainable trends in water and energy use. This nexus emanates from India’s policy of providing affordable calories to its large population. This requires that input prices are kept low, leading to perverse incentives that encourage groundwater over- exploitation. The paper argues that solutions to India’s groundwater problems need to be embedded within the current context of its water-energy-food nexus. Examples are provided of changes underway in some water-energy-food policies that may halt fur- ther groundwater depletion.

These lobbies, mostly comprised of midsized farmers, exerted considerable political influence on setting MSP prices for crops like paddy, wheat, and sugarcane. This wave of farmer politics came to be known as the “new agrarian movement,” where farmers unionized to bargain for higher MSPs and input subsidies (Rudolph and Rudolph 1987). The imperative to keep food prices low for urban consumers also meant that input subsidies had to continue so the cost of production for farmers could be kept low. Studies found that the availability of subsidized grains (rice and wheat) through PDS led to changes in the composition of traditional diets in many parts of India, away from the more nutritious nutri-cereals to less nutritious wheat and rice (Drèze and Khera 2017). India’s food policy, set in an era of food shortages and high food-price volatility, may be an obstacle to reforms in response to emerging challenges such as groundwater depletion, and high incidence of malnutri- tion, by providing perverse incentives to farmers to continue growing crops which are both water intensive and less nutritious.

knowledge.evidence: Two policy thrusts are particularly relevant from a water-use point of view. First is the inclusion of nutritious but low water-consuming food grains (Notaro et al. 2017), like nutri-cereals in some of the major public nutrition schemes such as midday meals in schools and the Integrated Child Develop- ment Scheme (ICDS; Drèze and Khera 2017). India’s poor performance in child nutrition outcomes (Deaton and Drèze 2009; Das, Sharma, and Babu 2018) has led to a renewed focus on nutrition in social security schemes (Drèze and Khera 2017). Recent policies such as the National Food Security Act of 2013 have included nutri-cereals as part of targeted PDS. There are also plans to serve nutri-cereals in schools as part of midday meals and at angaan- wadis (child care nurseries) as part of the ICDS in some states like Odisha (IANS 2019). There is some evidence to show that incorporating nutri-cereals in midday meals leads to better nutritional and cognitive outcomes for chil- dren (Anitha et al. 2019). Given the widespread concern about India’s nutri- tion deficit, more states are likely to promote nutri-cereals in their nutrition programs. This may incentivize farmers to grow less water-intensive crops.

knowledge.evidence: In view of the precarious groundwater situation in many Indian states, sev- eral initiatives have been undertaken to enhance groundwater supply or reduce its demand. Supply-side interventions have involved on-farm water harvesting through the construction of small ponds and tanks and related watershed management interventions (Everard 2015). While these have had significant impacts on water availability at the local scale, all water harvesting accomplishes at the basin scale is to reallocate water among users (upstream versus downstream), and among different hydrological units (groundwater versus surface water) without affecting the total amount of water in the system. Demand-side interventions, that is, interventions aimed at reducing demand for groundwater, have also been tried. These interventions include adoption of microirrigation technologies, laser levelers, and on-farm agricul- tural water management measures including conservation agriculture and SRI or “system of rice intensification” (Singh et al. 2015). Policy measures have also been tried such as the law to postpone the date of paddy transplan- tation in Punjab by one month to reduce groundwater pumping. It is not surprising that more than 80% of the roughly 180,000 SIPs in India are in states which already have a precarious groundwater condition (see figures 4 and 6). Evidence of the perverse WEF nexus policies in India can be seen in the paradoxical situation, where farmers in water scarce states have adopted SIPs, while farmers in water abundant eastern India have not. In the State of Rajasthan, SIPs have improved farm incomes, but overall groundwater extraction has increased substantially (Gupta 2019). Some states, like Gujarat, have introduced schemes whereby farmers can connect their SIPs to the electricity grid and sell excess electricity instead of pumping groundwater (Shah et al. 2018). A national scheme called Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha Utthan Mahabhiyan, more popularly known by its acro- nym KUSUM, also has a similar provision. Whether or not grid connection of pumps will reduce overall groundwater extraction remains a question. The answer will depend on several factors, including the price at which farmers can sell electricity.

knowledge.evidence: ABSTRACT: The impact of climate change on water balance components needs to be quantified from regional to local scale to manage water resources and suggest adaptation strategies to cope with future challenges. The present study was carried out to understand the climate change impact on water resources available at Krishna upper basin of India. CNRM RCM model was used to simulate the projections of rainfall and temperature with two RCP scenarios RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 and three time periods 2020-40 (near century), 2041-70 (mid-century) and 2071-99 (end century). It was observed that the change in mean annual rainfall projected by CNRM model under RCP 4.5 during 2020-40, 2041-70 and 2071-99 were 11.7, 26.7 and 32.2%, respectively and 18.6, 34.5 and 41.5%, respectively under RCP 8.5 scenarios. knowledge.evidence: The present study was conducted on Krishna upper sub-basin which comprises of Upper Krishna (K1), Middle Krishna (K2), Ghataprabha (K3) and Malaprabha (K4) sub-basins. The study area is situated between 15°3′to 18°6′ North latitudes and 73°39′to77°23′ East longitudes, extended in the states of Maharashtra and Karnataka. The total drainage area of the study area is about 54,228 km2 and has main outlet at Huvenhedigi in Raichur district of Karnataka. The elevation of study area ranges from 343 m to 1456 m with elevation difference of 1113 m. Geologically, the study area comprises of Deccan basaltic lava flows for upper cretaceous to lower Eocene age. Vertisols and laterites dominate soils in the basins (Deshpande, 1998). The high-altitude regions of the Western Ghats towards the western part of the study area experience more rainfall and the eastern part of the study area experiences semi-arid climate. The laterites are mostly found in high rainfall regions of Western Maharashtra and in the summits of the Deccan Traps. The location map of study area is given in Fig 1.

knowledge.evidence: ArcSWAT version 2012 was used for the study which is compatible and can add as a plugin with ArcGIS 10.3 version. The model set in the study focused on assessment of different water balance components and defines water availability with respect to space and time. The model was calibrated, validated with SWAT-CUP and was then used to assess climate change impact on water resources for future scenarios by selecting RCM models and by keeping the other variables constant. The detailed model inputs and setup was discussed in the paper published by Rao et al. (2023b). The calibrated and validated SWAT model was used to estimate the monthly water balance components at study area level and as well as major sub basins level. The historical water balance (1961-2019) using IMD gridded data was divided into two time slices. The present water balance and mean monthly water balance components were drawn from the average monthly water balance from the year 1991-2019. The monthly water balance components from the year 1961-1990 used as baseline period and compared with future time slicing periods such as 2020-2040, 2041-2070, 2071-2099 under climate change scenarios.

knowledge.evidence: The present study was conducted to make a detailed assessment of the variability and relationships of rainfall (mm) received, canal water (Mcum) supplied and the yield (kg/ha) of major crops viz., paddy, groundnut, sugarcane, sorghum and cotton crops attained under the Telugu Ganga Project (TGP) command area in Andhra Pradesh during 1997 to 2021. The crop productivity would always be influenced by the water resource available to a crop. Accordingly, linear and quadratic regression models of yield were calibrated to predict the yield of crops through canal water supplied in different years. The regression models were assessed based on the significance of coefficient of determination (R2) and magnitude of prediction error (PE) of the yield over years. The canal water released in different years was found to significantly influence the yield of paddy, groundnut, cotton and sugarcane crops under the TGP command area. The quadratic regression models gave higher and significant values of R2 compared to the linear regression models calibrated for different crops. The predictability of yield was found to be 0.725 under quadratic model compared to 0.605 under linear model for paddy, while it was 0.458 under quadratic model

source.title: Assessment of Variability of Rainfall and Canal Water under Telugu Ganga Project Command in

knowledge.evidence: Ganga Project (TGP) in Andhra Pradesh, a detailed assessment of the variability and relationships between the rainfall (mm) received, canal water (Mcum) supplied and the yield (kg/ha) of five major crops viz., paddy, groundnut, sugarcane, sorghum and cotton attained during 1997 to 2021 has been made in this paper. Linear and quadratic regression models were calibrated to assess the trends in the changes of annual rainfall, canal water released and yield of crops attained in different years. The models of yield were calibrated through the canal water supplied with the objective of assessing the effect of canal water on yield, apart from using the models for efficient prediction of yield attained in different years. The statistical criteria of coefficient of determination (R2) and prediction error (PE) of the yield were used to assess the efficiency of models for yield prediction. An increase in the release of canal water was found to significantly increase the yield of paddy, groundnut, cotton and sugarcane crops in different districts under the TGP command area. The quadratic regression models gave higher and significant values of R2 compared to the linear models of different crops.

source.title: Decision support system for efficient water management in canal command areas

knowledge.evidence: (CWREDSS) was developed to provide demand-based optimal canal water releases for reducing the gap between canal supplies and demands for increasing the water-use efficiency in canal command areas. The developed decision support system (DSS) was evalu ated under different situations of the command area of Guvvalagudem major distributary of the Nagar junasagar Left Canal, Andhra Pradesh, India, as a case study. Results indicate that the CWREDSS is capable of developing releases under different scenar ios of varying cropping patterns, groundwater use situations and different rainfall probability levels of the study area, and reduced the gap between demands and supplies considerably. DSS provides sugges tions/decisions under different situations of water deficit/surplus. CWREDSS will help irrigation engi neers, agronomists and agro-meteorologists in the planning, operation and management of irrigation systems.
knowledge.finding: Findings relate to groundwater, rainfall, water use efficiency.

knowledge.evidence: There are several sources of knowledge employed in the development of DSS. These sources are textbooks, manu als, research articles, personal experience and expert advice. The DSS was developed in the form of a com puter program using the input interactive controls and algorithms of Visual Basic 6.0 programing language. The nested 'If. .. Then . . . Else' construct was extensively used as in interactive algorithm for the generation of alternative decisions using the input information. Canal water releases at head works are the function of crop water requirement at field level, groundwater sup plies, seepage losses in canal network, canal geometry and water availability. While developing releases, all these components have to be estimated. Keeping these in mind, six modules were developed for the DSS, i.e. evapotranspiration (ET0), rainfall, crop, seepage loss, groundwater use and release module. source.title: Effectiveness of Dichanthium annulatum in Watercourses for Reducing Sediment Delivery from Agricultural Watersheds

knowledge.evidence: A field experiment was conducted to determine the efficacy of Dichantium annulatum grass filters in watercourses and to optimize the grass coverage in these watercourses. This experiment was conducted in 2% slope watercourses with varying filter grass coverage (0, 25, 50, 75, 100%) as main treatments and different flow rates (5, 10, 15, 20 L/s) as sub-treatments. The inflow and outflow, flow velocity, depth of the flow, and sediment concentration was measured and analyzed for each run. The experimental results reveal that the grass filter strips are able to reduce the sediment concentration in the runoff water by six times (from 4.2 to 0.65 g/L). The filter strips are able to reduce the velocity of the runoff water by two times (from 1.06 to 0.47 m/s) and convert the supercritical flows into subcritical flows. knowledge.evidence: A field experiment was conducted to determine the efficacy of D. annulatum grass filters in watercourses and to optimize the length of grass coverage in these watercourses. This experiment was conducted with different flow rates (5, 10, 15, and 20 L/s) and with varying grass coverage (0, 25, 50, 75, and 100%) in 2% slope watercourses (Fig. 2). The experiment was carried out with four replications. The watercourses were trapezoidal in shape with a bottom width of 0.6 m, depth of 0.45 m, side slope 1:1, and length of 30 m. For this experiment, D. annulatum was used as a vegetative filter in the watercourse. Dichanthium annulatum is a natural grass species in this region, which grows well and is very effective in controlling soil loss [33]. Dichanthium annulatum not only has a high soil binding ability, survival performance, water stable aggregation, but also has a promising fodder potential [34]. This is one of the best drought-resistant grasses for drought-prone areas in India. Dichanthium annulatum was planted as 100% coverage in July, during the monsoon season, and was allowed to grow for 60 days up to the flowering stage in September. The experiment was conducted for the above-mentioned grass coverage cuttings with different discharges.

knowledge.evidence: In semi-arid India, managed aquifer recharge (MAR) is often used to enhance aquifer storage, and by implication, water security, and climate resilience, by capturing surface runoff, mainly through check dams implemented at the community level. Despite their extensive use, the design of these structures typically does not follow a systematic method to maximize performance. To aid in the improvement of check dam design parameters and location siting, we develop a dynamic tool, which integrates the daily water balance of a check dam with analytical infiltration equations to assess check dam performance measured as temporal dynamics of storage, infiltration, and evaporation. The tool is implemented in R environment and requires meteorological and hydrogeological data, as well as check dam geometry and nearby well-abstractions, if any. The tool is applied to a case study in Saurashtra in Gujarat, where field visits were conducted. Simulations show that typical check dams in the area are able to store a volume between three and seven times their storage capacity annually. Some studies focus on estimating check dam performance from catchment-scale analysis. Methods include numerical groundwater modeling (Gore et al., 1998), remote sensing (Chinnasamy et al., 2015), and lumped hydrological modeling combined with before/after implementation analysis (Jain, 2012). Catchment-scale studies, however, have intrinsic difficulties in isolating the contribution of check dams to recharge from other components of the water balance. Regarding research on check dam performance at the structure-scale, some studies estimate recharge capacity from field-based observations using a water balance approach (Patel, 2002; Glendenning and Vervoort, 2010; Massuel et al., 2014; Dashora et al., 2018), the water table fluctuation method (Sharda et al., 2006; Renganayaki and Elango, 2013), or environmental tracers such as isotopes and chloride (Sharda et al., 2006; Stiefel et al., 2009; Massuel et al., 2014). The major limitation of field- based studies is the significant time and resources required.

Another limitation is that these assessments are based on existing structures and cannot easily be used for designing new structures. Abraham and Mohan (2019) used a 3-dimensional model developed in MODFLOW to evaluate the potential recharge from MAR interventions in Tamil Nadu at the structure- scale. The influence of groundwater level fluctuations on infiltration is crucial in semi-arid areas, where the water table can rapidly increase as a result of intensive rainfall events. Also, abstractions from nearby wells can induce a drawdown of the water table beneath the check dams, consequently increasing the infiltration rate. knowledge.evidence: Factors Affecting Infiltration The results of this study demonstrate that check dam infiltration is strongly influenced by the hydrogeological setting, the density of check dams, the geometry of the structure, and the dynamics of the water table. For sites over a permeable layer (condition A), water is free to move vertically beneath the weathered zone, therefore infiltrating more quickly compared to sites on an impermeable layer. In this case (condition B), downward movement is obstructed, and the water mound prevents further infiltration. The dynamics of the groundwater table are also crucial for infiltration rates (Figure 6), for which two different phases of infiltration can be identified: in the first phase of the filling at the unset of the monsoon, the water table is deep and therefore, hydraulically disconnected from the check dam (Equation 9); in the second phase, the water table is hydraulically connected with the check dam, and infiltration resembles the groundwater fluctuation (Equations 7, 8). This is in accordance with the infiltration model by Dillon and Liggett (1983), who studied the transition between disconnected water table conditions and hydraulic connections for infiltration.

knowledge.evidence: A new tool has been developed for assessing the performance of check dams for capturing water and storing it underground. The tool integrates the daily water balance of the check dam with a set of analytical infiltration equations and time series of groundwater table depth. The effective storage, infiltration, and losses by evaporation from a check dam can be simulated for different structure geometries and hydrogeological settings. The tool can satisfactorily simulate infiltration dynamics with validation results showing an average R2 of 0.93 between the simulated and measured water levels for a test case in Rajasthan, India. Based on a case in Rajkot district, Gujarat, the findings indicate that check dams have the potential to store up to seven times their storage capacity per year. It is demonstrated that the structure’s dimensions, the hydrogeological setting, and the maintenance of check dams play an important role in infiltration capacity, indicating that the selection of suitable locations and management are crucial to achieving the intended benefits of recharge structures. Results also show the complexity of recharge in semi-arid areas with large groundwater fluctuations and highlight the supremacy of models accounting

While groundwater has histori­ cally buffered surface water deficits, widespread overexploitation has precipitated aquifer depletion, land subsidence, and water quality deterioration. Conventional irrigation practices—characterized by low water-use efficiency and weak gov­ ernance—exacerbate these pressures. This review synthesizes principles and multi-scale applications of rainwater harvesting (RWH) as a strategic complement to conventional water management. It examines technical synergies between decentralized RWH systems and managed aquifer recharge (MAR), demonstrat­ ing their combined potential to alleviate stress on overexploited groundwater reserves. We address four objectives: (1) analyzing how increasing precipita­ tion variability and extreme climatic events destabilize agricultural systems and exacerbate water risk; (2) evaluating technical and managerial inefficiencies in conventional irrigation; (3) highlighting cascading environmental, economic, and social costs of groundwater overdraft; and (4) proposing an integrated RWH–

Temporally, precipitation is markedly seasonal and frequently epi­ sodic. A substantial proportion of the annual total, often 50–70%, occurs within a short, intense wet season. In the Zhifanggou Watershed of the Chinese Loess Plateau, for instance, rainfall is pre­ dominantly concentrated between June and September, accounting for 73.6% of the mean annual total and typically occurring as high- intensity, short-duration rainstorms that drive infiltration-excess runoff and severe soil erosion (Wu et al., 2018). This seasonal concen­ tration aligns poorly with crop water demand cycles. In response to groundwater depletion from over-extraction and the risk of saltwater intrusion in coastal zones, an increasing number of regions are implementing MAR projects using harvested rainwater or treated urban runoff. One method involves shallow basins constructed in areas with favorable soil permeability, where surface runoff or reclaimed water is impounded and gradually infiltrates to the underlying aquifer through diffusion and gravity. Another approach uses deep wells, either pre-existing or purpose- drilled, to directly convey rainwater or treated effluent into an aquifer. This method is particularly advantageous in urban settings where land availability is constrained. A third strategy enhances the infiltration capacity of specific river reaches or floodplains to utilize surplus wet- season flows for groundwater recharge. In arid and semi-arid regions, concentrated rainwater events often generate destructive flash floods. The strategic deployment of multiple RWH structures across a watershed can effectively attenuate peak flows during intense storms, reducing the frequency and severity of flood- related hazards. The integration of vegetative buffers with RWH struc­ tures further enhances water quality protection. Constructed wetlands, vegetative filter strips, and riparian buffers planted adjacent to RWH structures trap sediments, absorb excess nutrients, and facili­ tate the microbial degradation of organic contaminants. Microfinance models (e.g., Kenya’s Juhudi Kilimo program) have suc­ cessfully financed farm ponds with repayment tied to harvest cycles. Payment for ecosystem services (PES) schemes, where downstream water users pay upstream farmers for recharge-enhancing RWH, are being piloted in India’s Atal Bhujal Yojana. Public–private partner­ ships can co-finance large-scale MAR projects, reducing risk for pri­ vate investors. Governments should also consider water savings credit trading, allowing farmers who implement RWH to sell saved water quotas to industrial or urban users. In summary, a coordinated set of policy reforms, technological improvements, and governance shifts is pivotal to scale up RWH effec­ tively. By integrating RWH with data-driven irrigation, agroecological practices, and inclusive governance, stakeholders can realize a more resilient and equitable water future. This vision transcends traditional sectoral divisions, aligning water management with broader goals of agricultural productivity, ecosystem conservation, and climate adaptation.

This review has demonstrated that rainwater harvesting emerges not merely as an alternative water source but as a strategic imperative for building climate-resilient agricultural systems. knowledge.evidence: Indian agriculture is predominantly dependent on groundwater and consumes nearly 89% of its total groundwater draft. With recurrence of drought and faster depletion of groundwater resources in recent past, micro-irrigation technology has emerged to play crucial role in managing irrigation water demand and sustaining food security. The policy makers, recognising gravity of water scarcity across the Indian states, have focussed water policy pivotal to micro-irrigation. So, present study aims to estimate potential area across Indian states that are suitable for adoption of micro-irrigation. For estimation, sources of irrigation and crop suitability for micro-irrigation primarily under drip and sprinkler irrigation are considered across the states for year 2018–19. Based on different combinations of irrigation sources, estimate shows that country endows an area of 72–78 million ha on which micro-irrigation can be adopted. At country level, micro-irrigation penetration to our estimates ranges from 14.71–15.81% in recent years. Further, location coefficient reveals that concentration of micro-irrigation has improved over the years, however noticeable variation exists across the states. The states with dedicated agencies to improve micro-irrigation adoption

source.title: Integrated farming systems leveraging rainwater harvesting for enhanced productivity, profitability, and sustainability in hyper-arid regions of India

knowledge.evidence: Rainfed farming in hyper-arid regions faces significant challenges, including low productivity, poor economic returns and inefficient resource utilization due to erratic rainfall and limited diversification. The study was conducted during July 2019 to June 2023 at ICAR-Central Arid Zone Research Institute, Regional Research Station, Bikaner, Rajasthan to evaluate the productivity, profitability, and resource use efficiency of rainwater harvesting based Integrated Farming System (IFS) model with conventional cropping system of moth bean [Vigna acontifolia (Jacq.) Marechal] and cluster bean [Cyamopsis tetragonoloba (L.) Taub] under rainfed condition. Study assessed a 3.0 ha IFS model integrating arable crops, horticulture, fodder, dairy, vermicomposting, and mushroom cultivation, supported by rainwater harvesting. Results showed that compared to conventional sole cluster bean and moth bean cropping systems, IFS exhibited superior productivity with a mean Cluster Bean Equivalent Yield (CEY) of 7608 kg/ha, significantly surpassing the CEY of 274 kg/ha and 191 kg/ha under conventional rainfed cropping. The IFS achieved annual net returns of ₹1,79,899 with a B:C ratio of 2.40, representing 5.6 and 6.2 times higher net returns than sole cluster bean

Among arable crops, cluster bean demonstrated the highest profitability, with net returns of  ₹4,092 and a B:C ratio of  2.67, followed by moth bean (Supplementary Table 3). knowledge.evidence: The basic objective of water harvesting in high rainfall areas is to allow maximum possible rainwater to be stored in soil profile in-situ, and the excess runoff to be collected, stored and used in the same area or other areas. So, rainwater management in high rainfall areas involves creating a saturated soil profile, and storing water in ponds, ditches, streams and river beds. This helps in mitigating the water needs during dry spells in kharif season. Harvesting potential can be enhanced by integrating the check dams with ponds, and multi stage harvest with ponds. In high rainfall areas, the water storage structures are usually refilled in the same season with the subsequent rainfall, stream flow, spring water, or seepage water. The stored water in the soil profile and also in storage structures should be used judiciously by early sowing and promoting early growth, using crops with low water demand and deep rooting system, zero tillage or reduced tillage, residue recycling, and mulching. Rainwater productivity of the harvested water can be further enhanced by multiple use of water, and integration of water harvesting with seepage and evaporation management practices. Enhanced rainwater productivity due to water harvesting has associated benefits of groundwater

knowledge.evidence: Field bunds and management: In uplands, graded bunds should be provided across the slope, so that these act as a series of miniature barriers to check the loss of water and soil through runoff. The bund height should gradually increase from ~ 5-15 cm from upper reach to lower reach for rice crop. Previous studies reported that for medium lands, the optimum bund height is 20-25 cm for rice crop. Further, the runoff loss reduced substantially with 22 cm bund and with an increase in bund height, number of irrigations of 6 cm each during dry spells also reduced (Table 1). Bund management in terms of sealing in each season is required to check free flow through holes in bunds and additional return may be obtained from field bunds by growing crops such as pigeon pea, black gram, maize and yam in flood free areas. knowledge.evidence: Check dams: Temporary check dams are usually made from rocks, sandbags, concrete blocks, or wood. Permanent check dams are masonry structures and are very common. Sometimes, the masonry head wall of a permanent check dam is replaced with high quality folded rubber sheets anchored to masonry base which can be inflated and deflated to check and flush out sediments, respectively. ICAR-Flexi check dam: ICAR-flexi check dam or rubber dam is an inflatable structure built across a stream and used for water conservation, flood control and regulating flow of water in the stream. When it is inflated, it serves as a check dam/weir, while when deflated, it functions for flood mitigation and sediment flushing. Such flexi dams with a height from 0.5-1 m were tested across stream widths ranging from 2-5 m. The water stored in the upstream side of the dam extends to a length of 0.8-1.7 km. The additional volume of water stored in the upstream side varies between 4,800-10,000 m3 during monsoon season. In case the stored water is used for irrigation in dry spell, it gets continuously filled up by the water flowing from the upper catchment during monsoon. Harvesting potential can be enhanced by integrating the check dams with ponds in the storage

knowledge.evidence: Ahar and pyne system: The traditional system of ahar and pyne is one prominent practice in South Bihar. Ahar is the water harvesting structure and pyne is the diversion channel carrying the water to crop fields. Some pynes can be created by erecting embankment in the river beds. During dry spell, irrigation water for paddy crop is drawn out from Ahars by opening pipe outlets made at different heights in the embankment. Beds of ahar and pyne can used to grow a rabi crop using the residual moisture, especially in drought years in which the water level recedes fast. The system is also useful in groundwater recharge. Average area that can be irrigated from Ahar during kharif season is 57 ha and can go up to 400 ha.

knowledge.evidence: Indian agriculture is vulnerable to climate variability and change. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research through its network project on National Innovations on Climate Resilient Agriculture (NICRA) has demonstrated different land and water management interventions in the vulnerable districts of India to enhance the resilience of agriculture to climate change and variability. Rainwater harvesting and its judicious utilization through farm ponds and community tanks in rainfed districts demonstrated the ability to build resilience and also enhance cropping intensity (20–135%). Construction of temporary check dams (bori-bandhan) in high-rainfall areas brought lowland areas into cultivation which otherwise would have remained fallow due to inundation in the kharif (monsoon) season. knowledge.evidence: data on food grains, pulses, cereals and nutritious cereals in- dicate that despite higher deficits of rainfall, food grain pro- duction has stabilized, which could be due to stabilization of assured canal regions and increased use of groundwater. Pulse production continued to be dependent on rainfall. Though there is a general trend of a decrease in pulse pro- duction commensurate with deficit rainfall, spatial distribu- tion across the country plays an important role. A similar trend could also be observed with nutritious cereals. Total cereal production which includes paddy and wheat along with nutritious cereals is relatively stable despite a decrease in rainfall, indicating the preference for paddy and wheat cultivation in canal commands and using groundwater to a large extent. Floods are also a recurring phenomenon in India. Twenty-three of the 36 states and union territories in the country are subject to floods and 40 million ha of land, roughly one-eighth of the country’s geographical area, is prone to floods (Sikka et al., 2016a).

knowledge.evidence: India is more vulnerable to climate change in view of the de- pendence of its huge population on agriculture, excessive pressure on natural resources and poor coping mechanisms. Around 121 million ha (Mha) of the total geographical area (36.5% of the total) of the country are affected by various kinds of land degradation (National Academy of Agricul- tural Sciences (NAAS), 2010). Per capita availability of ar- able land has declined from 0.34 ha in 1961 to 0.13 ha in 2012 (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Na- tion’s statistical database (FAOSTAT), 2016). Per capita an- nual availability of water has declined from 5180 m3 in 1951 to 1540 m3 in 2011 (Central Water Commission (CWC), 2015) and is expected to reduce to 1340, 1150 and 1140 m3 by 2025, 2050 and 2065, respectively (Jain, 2011). The anticipated impact of climatic change and cli- mate variability including seasonality problems is likely to lead to increased pressure on already scarce water resources. Simulation studies on the impact of climate change on hy- drology and water resources have shown a varied response in Indian river basins depending upon the hydrological model, climate change scenarios and downscaling

knowledge.evidence: Different resource-conserving technologies (RCTs) such as zero or minimum tillage (with or without crop residues), bed planting of crops and direct-seeded rice have demon- strated substantial scope for improving irrigation efficiency and saving energy for groundwater pumping as well as re- ducing GHG emissions (Venkateswarlu et al., 2012). Direct-seeded rice (DSR) and zero-till wheat (ZTW) gener- ally gave a similar yield with less irrigation water and lower global warming potential (Figure 2). Intermittent irrigation with a ponding depth of 5 ± 2 cm of water in rice fields 3 days after disappearance (DAD) of pre- viously ponded water not only saves water but also reduces global warming potential by 25–30% over continuous flooding (Pathak, 2015; Chaudhari et al., 2015). Micro- irrigation options are not only important for saving water but also relevant for saving energy (Shah, 2009) and reduc- ing carbon emissions. Further, adoption of solar-powered drip systems results in water saving as well as energy saving and hence reduce carbon emissions. In eastern India, where groundwater is available at a shallow depth, solar pumps of- fer an ideal option for utilization of available groundwater

knowledge.evidence: As the frequency and intensity of floods are projected to in- tensify in the near future, a new management approach, Un- derground Taming of Floods for Irrigation (UTFI), has been demonstrated by the International Water Management Insti- tute (IWMI) to tackle the dual challenges of floods and groundwater depletion in the Rampur district of Uttar Pradesh. UTFI strategically recharges aquifers upstream during periods of high flow, thereby preventing local flooding and simultaneously building resilience by provid- ing additional groundwater for irrigation during the dry sea- son for livelihood improvement. It involves diverting excess floodwater from canals and recharging aquifers through well-designed recharge structures placed in ponds and other depression areas (Pavelic et al., 2015), and evacuated through large-scale pump irrigation during the dry season.

Traditionally, crops are irrigated with surface methods of irrigation that is, furrow, border, and basin irrigation. The majority of the farmers continue using these methods due to the lower infrastructure and operational costs involved. The various water-saving techniques such as alternate furrow irrigation (AFI), deficit irrigation (DI), and root zone drying irrigation, devised to improve water productivity and harvest quality, have been gradually, yet not widely, adopted over the years while complementing the conventional irriga- tion methods. The precise land levelling and well-maintained fields facilitate good irrigation schedul- ing practices, improve irrigation efficiencies, and reduce the wastage of water (Enciso et al., 2018). The recent progresses in laser land levelling practices enhance crop yield and water productivity and decrease labour requirement by reducing irrigation times because water distribution is even in a uniform field, which results in better seed germination, better crop growth, and higher crop yield (Jat et al., 2006). Therefore, improving the conveyance and application efficiencies in a surface irrigation system is a prerequisite for improving overall project efficiency and water productivity in the canal command area. Using pipes for conveyance and application eliminates all the associated losses, thereby increasing the project efficiency up to 89% (Wani et al., 2017). The success of a pressurized irrigation system in a canal command area relies upon the supply of water, switching from an on–off mode of water supply to a continuous water supply (Kumar et al., 2012). Thus, harvesting canal water into a reservoir in the field and reusing it through a pressurized irrigation system can improve water productivity in a canal- irrigated area, especially at the tail end. This rationale is supported by a study by Kumar et al. knowledge.evidence: GW has emerged as a reliable and easily obtainable source of irrigation in India. It has complemented the green revolution at Indian farms that utilized water- intensive high-yielding crop varieties and rigorous culti- vation practices (Shah, 1993). The use of GW resources for irrigation has seen a steep rise post independence (Figure 3). Much of this development happened in water-scarce basins and electrified places because of the inexpensive and unmetered electricity. The slow growth of the major irrigation projects of the country and poor maintenance of existing irrigation sources are also the reasons behind the steep rise in GW use (Moench, 2003). This source contributes about 44% of the total irrigation volume, but in return it provides nearly 60% of India's foodgrain production (Samra and Sharma, 2009; Shah, 2003). According to the GW law of India, this subject is a private entity, and the right for utilization belongs to the owner of that piece of land (Jeet, 2005). These systems include drip, bubbler, micro-sprinkler systems, etc., characterized by local (only root zone) application of irrigation water. However, delicate crops such as flowers and vegetables are generally not irrigated with sprinkler irrigation (M. Kumar et al., 2009). knowledge.evidence: The quality and certified standards (SI standards) of the irrigation equipment are important considerations for selection and installation in the field, especially when fertigation is to be done with the existing system. MI methods ensure high uniformity in water distribution and provide accurate irrigation scheduling until the system performs well. Thus, it becomes imperative to select the irrigation equipment that accurately suits the pedological, agronomical, and soil conditions of the field. The complexity of MI systems lies in their design and not in their operation (Kumar et al., 2009). For smooth opera- tion of the system, basic skills of the farmers, which may include maintenance, filter cleaning and changing, con- trolling emitter flow, and operating the flushing system, are required to enhance its life span. The major technical issue with MI operation in the field occurs due to clogging of emitters and lateral pipes with suspended sand, silt, and or algae entering with water and from the chemical precipitation of Mg and Ca, when irrigated with hard water. knowledge.evidence: There are three pillars for the successful adoption of MI technology on Indian farms: (a) economically viable and technically sound technology; (b) awareness towards the technology among the user group; and (c) selected tech- nology should be easily accessible by users (Namara et al., 2005). The major challenges in the adoption of MI faced by the farmers of the country are the high initial investment, delay in the subsidy distribution; uncertain government guidelines, difficult financing mechanism; poor follow-up services by agencies, as well as delays in the loan sanctioning process by banks (Namara et al., 2007). Out of these challenges, the high initial cost of investment secures the first rank for non-adoption of MI in the field by Indian farmers (Madhava Chandran and Surendran, 2016; Polak et al., 1997; Suresh et al., 2019). The central and state governments are work- ing closely to tackle such problems. The government has not only announced a large subsidy for MI but also is closely working with MI industries to control the unit costs of manufacturing. Such protocols should be compatible with exis- ting or improved management practices including irriga- tion, fertilization, pest management, and harvesting followed by farmers or recommended for the area. Many institutions have been working over the last few decades to improve the infrastructure of irrigation systems and management and utilization of irrigation water in India. Many WUA have been set up across the states of the county for inspection and man- agement of irrigation systems. Realizing the need of farmers in irrigation system management, the participa- tory irrigation management approach is practised in most of the states. The nation-wide target for doubling farmer income (DFI) in the DFI Committee Report (2018) rec- ommends achieving it by the judicious and scientific application of water. To support DFI, the PMKSY scheme of the GoI will bring more areas under the MI system as the objective of one of its schemes (“per drop more crop”). Under this scheme, a dedicated microirrigation fund with an initial corpus of Rs. 5,000 crores (Rs. 2,000 crores for 2018–2019 and Rs. 3,000 crores for 2019–2020) has been released to provide resources to the states for expanding coverage under MI.

knowledge.evidence: This paper reviewed the challenges of water manage- ment in farmers' fields in India and explores possibili- ties for higher irrigation use efficiency. A significant amount of water is lost in the conveyance and distribu- tion channels of the surface irrigation systems, resulting in poor irrigation efficiency in the field. Thus, system- atic maintenance of these channels, proper irrigation scheduling, precise land levelling, right cultivation methods, effective drainage, and efficient management of water by the farmers are the main focus areas for improving water productivity in the surface irrigation system. This review puts forth the potential of water- saving technologies such as, precision levelling, and automation in irrigation systems as reported by researchers. However, scaled studies of farmer's field conditions to support the findings of researchers are meagre. At the watershed level, the overall reduction in water consumption in irrigation is probably achieved when combinations of different water-saving technolo- gies are used by the irrigators. knowledge.evidence: The projected implications of climate change for water and agriculture to meet diverse and competitive water demands requires smart water management solutions. Science- and evidence-based, agricultural water management (AWM) can significantly contribute to reduce unsustainable water use and help enhance water resilience and adaptation to climate change. This paper presents a brief overview of potential AWM practices focusing on enhancing water resilience, increasing yields, and wherever possible, reducing emissions. This is achieved via increased land and water use efficiency, water and energy savings, and improved water productivity with considerable scope to improve agricultural resilience. In this context, the prioritization of a location-specific portfolio of smart AWM practices to make the right investment decisions is very important. We present two distinct and complementary approaches to pri- oritize AWM practices in this paper: one follows stakeholder analysis to build a prioritized portfolio of climate-smart AWM practices and the other employs a simple water balance-based approach to prioritize interventions. knowledge.evidence: With agriculture currently using 70% of freshwater resources globally and growing water demands from competing sectors, the food production system is increasingly exposed to the risks associated with water availability, quantity, and quality to support a growing population by 2050. Climate change is expected to intensify the existing risks, particularly in countries where water scarcity is already a concern (Iglesias & Garrote, 2015). The irrigated areas will increase in com- ing years, at the same time that more freshwater sup- plies will be diverted from agriculture to meet the increasing demands for water from the domestic, indus- trial, urban, and environmental sectors. In developing countries, where water extraction is often unregulated, unpriced, and subsidized, irrigated agriculture is placing increasing pressure on available freshwater resources (Fishman et al., 2015). This is particularly being felt in India, with a predominantly agrarian economy supporting about 18% of the global population with just 4.2% of the world's freshwater resources. Agriculture remains the predominant means of livelihood, employing over 50% of the Indian workforce and con- tributing about 17% to national gross domestic product

knowledge.evidence: Irrigation development in India has been a high priority since independence throughout the government's succes- sive 5-year plans. Huge investments were made in the development of canal irrigation, but this investment decelerated around the 1970s, and neglect of canal irriga- tion gave way to groundwater irrigation. Figure 1 shows the growth of irrigation by source in India. The net irri- gated area increased from nearly 18% in the early 1960s to about 48% in recent times (Jain et al., 2019). As evident from Figure 1, surface water from canals and tanks cov- ered most irrigated lands till about the late 1960s and early 1970s. With the advent of modern drilling and pumping technologies, government policies through sub- sidies, and rural energy supplies, groundwater develop- ment received a big boost. The number of groundwater irrigation structures went up from 6.2 million in 1986– 1987 to 20.5 million in 2013–2014 (Mukherji, 2020). Moreover, the area irrigated by groundwater has increased greatly: While it comprised only 29% of the total irrigated area in 1950–1951, today it accounts for 63% (Jain et al., 2019). knowledge.evidence: Groundwater has become a major source of irrigation, with 90% of withdrawal being used for irrigation and 63% of irrigated area using groundwater, leading to a serious risk of aquifers being overexploited. In India, out of the total 6,881 assessment units (blocks/mandals/talukas/ firkas), 1,186 units in various states (17%) have been cate- gorized as “overexploited,” indicating that groundwater extraction exceeds the annually replenishable groundwa- ter recharge. In addition, 313 units (5%) are “critical,” with groundwater abstraction ranging between 90% and 100% of the recharge (Central Ground Water Board [CGWB], 2019) (Figure 2b). In India, unsustainable groundwater (UGW) abstraction produces enough food to feed 173 million people, so losing access to UGW will aggravate food security concerns (Zaveri et al., 2016). A recent study shows that without any adaptations, based on the current trajectory of groundwater depletion, cropping intensity may decrease by 20% in India and by 68% in groundwater-depleted regions (Jain et al., 2021). The critical role of groundwater in building resilience in South Asian agriculture, with particular emphasis on India, has been discussed in Sikka et al. (2020).

With extreme weather expected to increase in the future because of climate change, the vulnerability of agricul- ture is also likely to increase. knowledge.evidence: As water is the medium of expression of the impacts of climate change, water management is at the centre of climate change adaptation (Sikka et al., 2018). Water is to adaptation what energy is to mitigation (United Nations, 2019). Climate-resilient agriculture refers to agricultural practices that enhance the capacity of the agroecosystem to relieve, resist, respond, and recover from climate-related disturbances. Conceptually, AWM is the management of water used in agriculture to enhance agricultural production with optimum water use. AWM has been defined in a variety of ways, mean- ing different things to different users. In a broader sense, AWM includes the management of water used in crop production (both rainfed and irrigated), livestock production, and inland fisheries (International Fund for Agricultural Development [IFAD], 2015). Water and land management is one of the major pathways to enhancing resilience and reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in agriculture as well. Many researchers in India have demonstrated how the promotion of innovative AWM interventions can build resilience to climate change (Anantha et al., 2020; Jat et al., 2020; Patle et al., 2019; Sikka et al., 2016, 2018). The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), through its various institu- tions, and the All India Coordinated Research Project on Irrigation Water Management (AICRP-IWM), state agri- cultural universities (SAU), water and land management institutes (WALMI) in the states, the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), and other CGIAR (formerly the Consultative Group for International Agri- cultural Research) centres have contributed to bringing out area- and crop-specific improved AWM practices to increase water use efficiencies, water productivity, and to build resilience. knowledge.evidence: Alternate wetting and drying method of irrigation Another recommended irrigation alternative for irrigated rice systems is alternate wetting and drying (AWD). Under AWD, rice fields are subjected to alternate cycles of saturated and unsaturated conditions where irrigation is interrupted and water is allowed to subside until the ponded water disappears and the soil reaches a certain moisture level (Carrijo et al., 2017). AWD can reduce irri- gation water inputs by 23%–43% and can reduce the GWP by 45%–90% as compared to continuously flooded rice (Adhya et al., 2014). Pathak (2015) reported a reduc- tion in GWP by 25%–30% using intermittent flooding in rice over continuous flooding. knowledge.evidence: Optimizing irrigation scheduling Irrigation scheduling helps to optimize the application of the right amount of water at the right time and place to optimize crop production, conserve water, and improve performance of irrigation systems. The major finding from a comprehensive review by Sapkota et al. (2020) suggests that optimizing irrigation schedules may help to reduce methane (CH4) emissions and net GWP. With appropriate irrigation scheduling, optimum soil water conditions for plant growth are maintained and a sub- stantial amount of water is saved. Proper irrigation scheduling also leads to efficient use of fertilizers, thus reducing GHG emissions as well. In India, region-specific irrigation scheduling for major crops has been docu- mented based on field experiments under ICAR-AICRP on water management for surface irrigation and micro- irrigation (All India Coordinated Research Project on Irrigation Water Management (AICRP-IWM), 2019). There have also been experimental studies on evapo- transpiration (ET)-based irrigation scheduling based both on measured actual ET and computed ET (Hunsaker et al., 2015). knowledge.evidence: Water productivity in canal command areas Improving agricultural water productivity in canal com- mand areas through AWM interventions, both technical and institutional, can help close the growing gap between the IPC through irrigation projects and their actual utili- zation. One novel approach to increasing economic water productivity (EWP) in canal command areas has been demonstrated by Amarasinghe et al. (2021) in the water- scarce Sina irrigation system in the semi-arid district of Ahmednagar in Maharashtra to enhance resilience. This approach uses EWP and the water cost curve as tools to reallocate irrigation-consumptive water use and identify economically viable cropping patterns and AWM under different scenarios (normal, dry, and wet years). The results of this study suggest that the cropping patterns that include high-value, water stress-tolerant crops such as orchards (pomegranate, etc.) with micro-irrigation can be a permanent component in the cropping pattern to provide sustainable income even in low-rainfall years. knowledge.evidence: Rainwater harvesting for managed aquifer recharge Soil moisture security and enhanced water storage through water harvesting in surface and subsurface stor- age structures helps improve resilience at the local level in farming systems. Rainwater harvesting and its judi- cious utilization through farm ponds and community tanks in rainfed districts demonstrated this ability and enhanced cropping intensity (20%–135%) (Sikka et al., 2018). A recent study of drought-prone watersheds in central India showed that rainwater harvesting through surface water storage (the haveli system), check dams, and field infiltration structures led to an increase in groundwater levels by 2–5 m, providing water security in dry years. In addition, crop yields increased by 10%– 70%, 20% of fallow lands were brought under cultivation, and overall household income increased by 1740 US $/year on average (Garg et al., 2020). Similarly, the bene- fits of large-scale adoption of managed aquifer recharge through rainwater harvesting is being widely reported (Patel et al., 2020).

knowledge.evidence: Conjunctive water use Conjunctive water use refers to the coordinated and planned utilization of surface water and groundwater resources in an integrated manner appreciating interdependence as well as different characteristics of the two water sources. Conjunctive water use management is more effective than focusing on surface water or ground- water in isolation. Irrigation systems should promote conjunctive irrigation of surface and groundwater by design and not by default to reduce the impact of climatic risks on agriculture and income resilience. One novel way of implementing conjunctive water use management has been successfully piloted in the Gangetic basin, where rainfall is concentrated in 3–4 monsoon months, through an approach known as “Underground Transfer of Floods for Irrigation” (UTFI) (Alam & Pavelic, 2020; Pavelic et al., 2015). UTFI involves strategically installing managed aquifer recharge infrastructure to recharge depleted aquifers with excess wet-season flows that might pose flood risk to a river basin. This both alleviates the flood risk and increases the groundwater available for irrigation (Pavelic et al., 2015). knowledge.evidence: The stakeholder participatory approach developed by Khatri-Chhetri et al. (2019) was used to prioritize inter- ventions to develop district-level climate adaptation plans for resilient farming in India under the project “Strength- ening Capacity in India for Scaling-up Climate-Smart Agriculture Technologies, Practices and Services” (ICAR, IWMI, CCAFS, 2020). Here we present the application of the stakeholder prioritization process for the Adilabad District of Telangana, India. The average annual rainfall of the district is 1,146 mm, and 85% of rainfall occurs during the south-west monsoon season (June– September). The district is primarily rainfed, and only 25% of the cultivated area is irrigated. Climate data analy- sis and stakeholders identified rainfall deficit, dry spells, and extreme rainfall events to be the main risks. Climate data analysis showed 70% of the total district area is drought prone, and 22% of the total district area is prone to extreme rainfall, with dry spells varying in duration from 11 to 24 days. During the stakeholder workshop, the district's climatic risks were ranked on a 0–5 scale, where 0 indicates no risk, 1 is very low risk, 2 is low risk, 3 is medium risk, 4 is high risk, and 5 is very high risk.

knowledge.evidence: Expanding smart AWM at scale has been an issue, and awareness and capacity building are the key constraints in improving adaptive capacity to scaling out resilient interventions. An innovative approach to capacity build- ing under the ClimaAdapt Project was implemented from 2012 to 2016 to improve the adaptive capacity of stakeholders and farmers' groups in the Krishna River basin, India (Kakumanu et al., 2019). The study was taken up under the Nagarjuna Sagar Project in the selected command areas in the Nalgonda District of Telangana and the Guntur District of Andhra Pradesh, covering 178 farmers. AWD in rice, a modified system of rice intensification (MSRI) and DSR were the key climate-resilient AWM interventions selected for imple- mentation and capacity building. knowledge.evidence: AWM to enhance water resilience and adaptation to cli- mate change is critical to sustain agriculture, especially in already water-stressed areas. Management of water and land is one of the main pathways for improving yield, enhancing resilience, and in most cases, reducing GHG emissions—the three pillars of CSA. Field-based evidence from a number of studies have demonstrated that water demand and supply management AWM practices and technologies (DSR, LLL, AWD, drip irrigation, CA, sub- surface drip, optimized irrigation scheduling, BBF system, water harvesting and aquifer recharge) significantly con- tributed to enhancing resilience via reduced non- beneficial losses and increasing land and water use effi- ciency, thereby conserving more water, increasing or maintaining yields, and reducing energy and fertilizer usage, thus also reducing GHG emissions. knowledge.evidence: portfolio of smart AWM practices for making the right investment decisions is an important task. We showcase the application of the two distinct but complementary pri- oritization approaches: stakeholder analysis and a simple water balance-based approach for prioritization of AWM interventions. We suggest that the two approaches should possibly be used together to complement each other. The stakeholder participatory process can provide a suitable portfolio of practices obtained through a bottom-up approach, whereas the water balance model can quantify the impact of these practices on climate-smart metrics (yield, resilience, emissions, economic benefits). Expanding smart AWM at scale has been an issue, and capacity building, extension services, and the conver- gence of resources and institutions are among the key constraints. There is evidence to support the impact of capacity building for institutions responsible for water management and farmer groups. source.title: Drivers and Challenges of Micro‐Irrigation Adoption and Intensity in India: A Study of Four States

knowledge.evidence: India's food security relies substantially on groundwater, but inefficient irrigation is seriously depleting this resource. Micro-­ irrigation (MI) improves irrigation application efficiency and productivity, yet adoption remains low. This study examines MI adoption across four major Indian states—Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Telangana—using primary data, Heckman's two-­stage regression and perception analysis. The sample is drawn from farmers with independent water sources, and the findings should be interpreted within this scope. The study identifies key determinants of adoption, including access to information, high-­value crop cultivation, wild animal damage, landholding size and subsidies. High investment costs and en- ergy requirements remain significant barriers, particularly for smallholders. Strengthening information dissemination, easing subsidy access, improving fencing and promoting land consolidation can boost MI adoption. Implementing these measures will improve irrigation efficiency and contribute to sustainable agriculture and long-­term food security.

Groundwater sup- ports over 60% of the country's agriculture, and extraction rates have surpassed natural replenishment and led to poor ground- water development (MoWR 2017; Bhattarai et al. 2021). The state of groundwater extraction in the key food-­producing states— Haryana (134%), Punjab (166%), and Rajasthan (151%)—is signifi- cantly above the replenishment rates, while Madhya Pradesh (MP) (59%), Maharashtra (55%), Telangana (42%) and Uttar Pradesh (UP) (60%) are at margins of replenishment rates (CGWB 2023). The demand for freshwater is likely to swell further because of global megatrends: population growth, rapid urbanization, the emerging middle class and their increased affluence, growing in- equality and climate change (Bates et al. 2008; King et al. 2017).

knowledge.evidence: The irrigation application efficiency in Indian agriculture is estimated at approximately 35%–40% under canal-­based sys- tems and approximately 60% under groundwater-­based irri- gation at the field level (Chand et  al.  2020). It is important to distinguish application-­level efficiency from basin-­level water use efficiency, which accounts for return flows and recycling. The case for MI adoption rests not only on field-­ level efficiency gains but also on the ‘dry water savings’ con- cept (Seckler 1996), that is, while return flows from surface irrigation may be recirculated within a basin, groundwater depletion from overextraction represents genuine nonrecov- erable loss. MI reduces nonbeneficial evaporation and deep percolation, losses that cannot be recaptured, unlike surface return flows, while improving water control and beneficial evapotranspiration. However, these water-­saving impacts are not uniform and are conditioned by the geo-­hydrological en- vironment, crop type, climate and MI technology deployed (Kumar 2016).

knowledge.evidence: Micro-­irrigation (MI) has been found to enhance returns from high-­value crops by increasing yield and quality, reducing elec- tricity consumption, increasing nitrogen use efficiency, present- ing climate mitigation benefits, saving labour and adapting to varied terrains (Namara et al. 2005; Kumar 2016; Reddy 2016; Gandhi et al. 2021; Zhang et al. 2021; Pronti et al. 2024). Some re- search indicates a possible rebound effect in MI adoption, where efficiency gains may lead to an increase in absolute water use due to increased irrigated area (Scott et al. 2014; Song et al. 2018; Singh et al. 2024). Nevertheless, for the highly populous nation, enhancing agricultural productivity while managing depleting groundwater resources remains imperative, both to ensure the long-­term sustainability of its food system and to safeguard na- tional food security.

knowledge.evidence: To accelerate the adoption of MI, the Indian government consolidated various schemes under Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana in 2015 with a budget of Rs. 500 billion ($5.95 billion) over 5 years. Despite significant policy efforts to promote MI, its adoption remains low. MI adoption is predomi- nantly driven by the following: (a) the cultivation of high-­value row crops (fruits, vegetables and flowers) where the return on MI investment is clearly positive, (b) farm-­level water scar- city where conventional irrigation is severely constrained and (c) agro-­ecological conditions favorable to drip/sprinkler application (Kumar, Turral, et al. 2008; Kumar 2016; Gandhi et al. 2021; Mohan et al. 2024). In cereal-­dominated, canal-­ irrigated settings, the economic incentive to adopt MI is con- siderably weaker, partly explaining the persistent adoption gap in these states. The substantial spatial and agro-­ecological heterogeneity in MI adoption across Indian states is presented in Table 1 and visually in Figure 1.

Adoption is relatively high in states such as Karnataka (84%), Maharashtra (75%), Andhra Pradesh (66%), Mizoram (57%) and Tamil Nadu (49%). In contrast, large agrarian states that are central to na- tional food security, including Punjab (2%), UP (3%), Bihar (4%), West Bengal (3%) and MP (9%), exhibit very low MI penetra- tion relative to their extensive net irrigated areas. UP and MP together make an outsized contribution to India's agricultural output, accounting for approximately 31% of total foodgrain pro- duction, 37% of pulses and 27% of oilseeds. UP alone contributes nearly 47% of national sugarcane production.

knowledge.evidence: We employed two analytical approaches to examine MI adoption data: the Heckman two-­stage regression and a perception analysis. To avoid selection bias of the data, we adopted the Heckman two-­ step model. The Heckman model first estimates adoption probabil- ity using a probit regression (Equation 1) and then applies ordinary least squares (OLS) to analyse technology intensity (Equation (2)). The inverse Mills ratio (IMR) corrects for selection bias, ensuring robust estimation. Key explanatory variables include farmer de- mographics, land characteristics, access to credit, subsidies and information. Prior to running the model, we checked for multicol- linearity, normality and homoskedasticity.

knowledge.evidence: In the second-­stage regression analysis, we examined factors influencing technology intensity, defined as the percentage of farmland brought under MI. Key determinants included crop concentration, farmer size, land fragmentation and state-­wise variations. The Herfindahl index (β = 20.49, p = 0.002) showed that farmers with concentrated cropping patterns expanded MI more, likely because such specialization often involves high-­value crops supported by established market linkages. Conversely, land fragmentation (β = −2.19, p = 0.022), which initially appeared to encourage adoption, was found to hinder intensive use and expansion due to water supply, road and elec- tricity access constraints in fragmented holdings. Market dis- tance (β = −0.2287, p = 0.094) was negatively associated with expansion, as proximity to markets facilitates input access and output sales. Table 6 shows that the mean MI area increases steadily with farm size from 0.76 ha for marginal farmers to 8.15 ha for large farmers, while the proportional intensity falls from 94% to 57%. State-­level factors mattered, with Maharashtra (β = 36.26, p < 0.001) and Telangana (β = 34.93, p < 0.001) show- ing higher adoption intensity than UP, likely due to stronger institutional support and greater water scarcity in these states.

knowledge.evidence: Table 7 reports farmers' perceptions of MI potential, effective demand and supply. The results indicate that agronomic poten- tial plays a key role in MI adoption. As per total agreement % in Table 7, all respondents agreed that MI improves yield, while 99% acknowledged water savings, 68% acknowledged labour re- duction and 57% acknowledged fertilizer savings. Better weed control under MI was agreed by 75%, and 43% agreed on lower incidence of pests after MI adoption. These findings reinforce the technology's agronomic benefits as a major driver. The re- sults showed that 94% believed MI increases profitability, 92% saw improved product quality and 63% noted reduced input costs. While 90% valued subsidies, 35% found capital costs of MI as high, indicating affordability concerns for some despite expected returns. In effective demand factors, 92% considered the technology easy to use, and 90% confirmed good informa- tion availability on MI. However, water availability and elec- tricity reliability (71% and 62%, respectively) were indicated as important concerns. knowledge.evidence: Figure 4 highlights the results on key challenges in adopting MI. The top concerns of farmers were damage to MI laterals and crops from wild animals (64%), lack of fencing (60%), which could prevent animal intrusion. Animals such as wild boars, blue bulls, squirrels and rats are reported to frequently damage MI, causing losses and crop failure, making fencing important for adoption. A declining groundwater table (45%) is also an im- pending challenge, alongside high well and tubewell installation costs (43%), limited credit access (40%) and difficulties in obtain- ing subsidies (39%). As farmers pump water from deeper levels, costs rise because larger pumps are needed, and high-­TDS water can clog laterals when drip lines dry in the sun (Kumar 2016), discouraging adoption.

knowledge.evidence: Larger landholdings may involve more fragmented parcels, but they also increase farmers' capacity to invest regardless of frag- mentation. Evidence shows that farmers with larger landhold- ings are more likely to adopt new technologies (Madramootoo and Morrison 2013; Ruzzante et al. 2021). They have better fi- nancial resources, access to credit and extension and a greater ability to manage risk, which supports adoption. While land fragmentation complicates irrigation management, large farm- ers perceive the benefits of MI—profitability, cost reduction, and increased yields—as outweighing these challenges. The positive association of the Herfindahl index with adoption re- flects farmers' tendency to concentrate on high-­value crops amenable to MI rather than monoculture per se (Kumar, Turral, et al. 2008; Fishman et al. 2023). Crop type and value are the un- derlying drivers of adoption; the Herfindahl index captures this indirectly, as farmers growing such crops naturally tend toward concentration.

knowledge.evidence: The study finds adoption across all farm sizes, with higher in- tensity among small farms. The lower proportional intensity among large farmers reflects a denominator effect, where the share under MI declines as total operated land increases, even though the absolute area continues to rise. Our research con- firms that groundwater-­dependent farmers show a greater propensity to adopt MI than those relying on other sources, unsurprisingly, since drips and sprinklers are poorly suited to canal irrigation. The mismatch between surface water delivery schedules (once every 10–15 days) and MI's requirement for fre- quent, low-­volume applications necessitates costly intermediate storage and pumping infrastructure, undermining economic vi- ability (Kumar 2016). Even among groundwater users, adoption remains constrained where farmers depend on water purchase or where poor groundwater quality, as varying total dissolved solids levels reaching up to 2000 ppm in parts of India, causes dripper clogging and system failure. While expanding tubewell installation is inadvisable, any new groundwater source should be accompanied by policies that actively encourage water con- servation and MI adoption. knowledge.evidence: Analysing technology adoption intensity reveals the impact of factors such as smaller fragmented plots, soil type, market accessibility and farm size on the adoption of MI. Farmers cultivating a single high-­value crop are more likely to expand MI coverage due to economies of scale and comparative ad- vantage over cereal crops. Conversely, farmers with smaller plots face compounding infrastructure constraints, such as a lack of independent water sources, electricity and road access, that hinder scaling, often pushing them toward water mar- kets (Kumar, Turral, et al. 2008). These findings echo broader structural barriers to MI adoption—the dominance of small and marginal farmers, mismatched water delivery schedules in canal commands, poor groundwater quality in arid regions and weak extension—and subsidy administration collectively limits uptake beyond well-­endowed, commercially oriented farms. We learned that farmers are also cautious about scal- ing due to potential crop damage from animals such as blue bulls, boars, stray cattle and rats. Adoption of MI would re- quire additional investments in wire fencing to protect crops, leading farmers to assess the cost–benefit carefully. Market

knowledge.evidence: The study relies on recall data from adopters and nonadopters, which may affect response accuracy. Land fragmentation was measured using a Likert scale, although an index such as the Simpson Index could allow for clearer analysis. Fragmentation is largely shaped by inheritance and demographic factors; therefore, reverse causality is unlikely, but omitted variables such as land markets or local irrigation norms may bias esti- mates. The Heckman approach corrects for sample selection but does not fully resolve endogeneity. Future work using in- strumental variables or panel data would strengthen causal inference. Water scarcity was captured through a perception-­ based ordinal proxy rather than a quantitative measure such as season-­wise irrigated area. Future studies should collect season-­specific irrigation data to build stronger farm-­level in- dicators. The purposive sample includes mainly subsidy bene- ficiaries with independent irrigation sources, excluding those who buy water, share wells or depend on surface systems, so findings should be read within this scope. Network effects were not captured, and COVID-­19 restricted follow-­up sur- veys. A larger nonadopter sample would improve robustness.
